### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Umansky, Avelar, and Thompson (2026) establish something new and reliable: a statewide, population-level portrait of how much credit-bearing instructional time secondary EL-classified students in Oregon carry relative to non-EL peers in the same school, grade, and year. On that measure the EL population as a whole carries fewer core credits than its peers (−0.21 credits; −0.02 total), only about 18% of EL student-years exceed the +0.5-credit threshold, and when EL students do carry a surplus, roughly two-thirds of it lands in electives and ELD rather than core content, with about a third of recipients still short of a full core load. The peer-relative credit differential itself — program-agnostic, built from routine SCED-coded course records, portable to other states — is a genuine methodological contribution, and the paper's Discussion supplies the interpretive key the abstract omits: much of what is labeled 'extra instructional time' is probably a fuller schedule for students who cannot afford to lighten their load, not a supplemental program. The causal half is considerably weaker than the abstract's 'substantially increased' language implies. The course-taking 'effects' in Table 6 are close to an accounting decomposition of the treatment variable (subject coefficients sum to roughly 0.9 of each marginal credit), and the full-course-load odds ratios are both mechanical and estimated only on students who switch status. The graduation result — the paper's most quotable claim — rests on a matched sample of roughly 1,300 (under 900 for five-year outcomes) whose Ns cannot be reconciled with the stated sample or retention rates, is non-monotone across specifications (CEM with student controls erases it; adding school and cohort fixed effects to small logits revives it), is exposed to reverse causality through persistence and to circularity through Oregon's modified-diploma track, reaches significance in only two of sixteen regular-diploma cells (one at p < .1), and disappears entirely when regular and modified diplomas are pooled (Appendix A7). The achievement models are the best-identified estimates and their near-null result is credible as 'no large effect detected,' though measurement error, reclassification-driven attrition, and repeated coursework all bias toward zero. Layered on top is an unusual density of text–table disagreements (a mistyped odds ratio, a wrong percentage conversion, unreconciled sample counts, a mislabeled Table 8 panel, five different significance-star conventions, two incompatible definitions of 'displacement') and no data availability statement, code, or named software. All five sub-reviews converge: the descriptive and measurement contributions are solid and should be absorbed by the field; the causal headlines should be cited only in the hedged form the authors themselves use in the body. Cite this paper for what secondary EL students' schedules look like relative to peers, for the allocation of surplus time to electives, for the precise achievement null, and for the 'fuller schedules as an invisible allocation lever' argument. Do not cite it as evidence that extra instructional time raises graduation, or as an evaluation of any extended-day, summer, or tutoring program.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The count is wrong. Under Table 8's own legend (** p < .05, * p < .1), seven of the sixteen regular-diploma cells are starred: for four-year core credits 1.425**, 1.48* and 1.464*; for five-year any credits 1.697**, 1.774** and 1.792**; and for five-year core credits 1.814**. Every star is consistent with its standard error. In the preferred Matching 3 column two of four cells are starred (1.464, p = .059; 1.792, p = .017). Supplemental Appendix A7 confirms no effect when regular and modified diplomas are pooled, and all eight modified-diploma cells are significant, so the abstract's claim survives in weakened form as a shift from modified to regular diplomas. On the sample sizes, Supplemental Table A2 gives matched Ns of 1,544, 1,502 and 1,024; Table 8's Ns are 71–90% of these and undocumented, and the text's 77%/72% retention rates match nothing. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table and the supplement.

#### Key Strengths

- A novel, reusable measure: extra instructional time operationalized as a student's enrolled credits minus the mean of non-EL peers in the same school, grade, and year (binary flag at +0.5 credits), built from routine SCED-coded course records. It detaches the study of extra time from named programs and is portable to any state with course-level data; the authors' own inference that schools differentially allocate time through 'fuller schedules' is the paper's sharpest and most transferable idea.
- A population-level descriptive portrait that did not previously exist, and its most important feature is the negative baseline: EL-classified secondary students in Oregon on average carry fewer core credits (−0.21) than same-school/grade/year non-EL peers, no subgroup closes the core-content gap, and only ~18% of student-years exceed the +0.5-credit threshold. The '18% get extra time' figure sits inside a systematic deficit.
- The allocation finding is clean, transparent, and policy-relevant, and it does not depend on any causal claim: among EL students with extra time the surplus is +0.61 elective and +0.11 ELD credits versus +0.23 across all four core subjects combined (Table 5), and roughly a third of extra-time recipients are still not in a full core course load.
- A well-powered, honestly interpreted achievement null: student, grade-by-year, and school fixed effects on ~27,400 student-years with standard errors around 0.008 SD; the single surviving estimate (0.022 SD, ELA, core credits) is benchmarked against Kraft (2020) and correctly called below policy relevance rather than spun.
- Unusual candor about the design's limits: the Discussion concedes that much measured 'extra time' is probably fuller schedules and reports that state leaders pushed back on the supplemental-program reading; the failed generalized-propensity/IPW approach is disclosed in an appendix rather than buried; reclassification is correctly treated as post-treatment and probed rather than matched on; and summer/online format estimates are labeled lower bounds after participant checks.

#### Key Concerns

- The construct does not identify what the title and abstract promise. 'Extra instructional time' is a relative credit differential, not receipt of supplemental instruction, and the paper's own tables show the two diverge: 12th graders take the fewest total and core credits of any grade yet are most often flagged (53%), because non-EL seniors reduce their loads. The grade-12 surplus is entirely non-core (Table 3: +0.384 any vs. −0.031 core), so the claim that extra time is 'concentrated in the last 2 years... to support graduation' is most likely a comparison-group artifact. The 86% 'longer school day' format is a residual category, not an observed program.
- The course-taking 'effects' are close to arithmetic identities and the full-course-load result is mechanical. Table 6 regresses subject-area credits on the total credit differential from which they are built; Model 3 coefficients sum to 0.88 (middle school) and 0.95 (high school). Taking more credits mechanically raises the odds of holding all four core classes, and the FE logit uses only switchers (4,857 of 26,461 and 5,007 of 12,104 student-years). The abstract's 'substantially increased the likelihood of enrolling in a full course load' inherits both problems.
- The graduation result is the weakest analysis in the paper and the source of the headline. Small matched samples (845–1,383) whose Ns match neither the stated 2,130 nor the 77%/72% retention rates; estimates that collapse under CEM-plus-controls and revive only when school and cohort fixed effects enter small logits (an incidental-parameters signature); a treatment ('extra time in 2+ high school years') that partly encodes persistence; diploma-track circularity (the modified diploma requires fewer core credits by design); a post hoc dichotomization with no threshold sensitivity; 32 unadjusted cells with two regular-diploma hits (one at p < .1); and Appendix A7 showing no effect on graduating when diploma types are pooled. The body calls this 'exploratory' and 'tentative'; the abstract and conclusion do not.
- Text–table disagreements dense enough that no number in the prose can be quoted without checking the exhibit: the Data section's 32,673 / 64,162 versus Tables 1–2's 32,685 / 64,241; Table 3's unexplained N of 53,311; 'OR = 0.0464' for Table 8's 0.464; '88% lower' for an OR of 0.175 (82.5%); '0.010 SD' for a coefficient in no column of Table 7; a Table 8 panel headed 'Four-year' that reports five-year results; five different significance-star conventions with Tables 3 and 8 carrying no legend; a Discussion claim of 'roughly equal' core/non-core allocation that Table 5 contradicts by about 3:1; and a 'progressive distribution' claim (including ELs with disabilities) that holds only in the 'any' specification and reverses for core.

  > **Correction (2026-09-25).** The claim that Tables 3 and 8 carry no significance legend is wrong: all five tables have legends. The accurate statement is that the paper uses four distinct legend schemes, so a single asterisk denotes three different thresholds across tables. The advice to read each table's note before interpreting stars stands. Confirmed against the rendered tables.

- Verification is blocked by missing infrastructure and ambiguous construction: no data availability statement, no code, no named software or CEM implementation, no SCED-to-subject crosswalk, no statement of whether former ELs count as non-EL peers or of any minimum peer-cell size, two incompatible definitions of the 'displacement' statistic (lacking one core class vs. lacking all four), and two incompatible descriptions of the fixed-effects structure (grade-by-year plus school vs. school-by-year). The achievement z-scores' standardization reference is deferred entirely to an unseen appendix.

#### What to Rely On

- EL-classified secondary students in Oregon (2013-14 to 2018-19) enrolled on average in 0.21 fewer core-content credits and about the same total credits (−0.02) as non-EL peers in the same school, grade, and year; the core deficit is deepest for beginning-ELP students (−0.76). This is transparent arithmetic on administrative data, consistent across Tables 1 and 2, and corroborates the authors' earlier multistate work.
- Only about 17–18% of EL student-years exceed the +0.5-credit threshold relative to same-school/grade/year non-EL peers ('any' and 'core' versions). Cite this as a peer-relative credit-load statistic, not as a program-participation rate, and note that it is a share of student-years rather than of students.
- When EL students carry surplus credits, most of it goes to electives and ELD rather than core content (+0.61 elective, +0.11 ELD, +0.23 across all four core subjects; Table 5), and roughly a third of extra-time recipients are still not enrolled in a full core course load. The share structure in Table 6 (about 45–48% of each marginal credit to electives, 37–45% to core, 7–13% to ELD) is the defensible reading of that table.
- Within-student changes in credit load are not associated with policy-relevant test-score gains: at most 0.022 SD in ELA (core credits) and nothing detectable in math, with standard errors tight enough to rule out effects above roughly 0.03 SD per credit. The defensible phrasing is 'no large positive achievement effect detected,' not 'extra time does not improve achievement.'
- The measurement idea itself, and the conceptual claim that schedule fullness is an under-studied lever by which schools differentially allocate instructional time. This is likely to be the paper's most durable contribution.
- Identifiable alternative delivery formats are rare in these data: summer (5%), online (1.4%), and concurrent enrollment (3.2%) account for a small share of extra-time cases, as acknowledged lower bounds. The residual 'longer school day' category should not be read as evidence of extended-day programs.
- EL-classified students are substantially over-represented among Oregon's modified-diploma earners (Study Context), and the modified diploma forecloses four-year college enrollment — a stratification mechanism invisible in federally reported graduation rates.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- 'Extra instructional time substantially increased the likelihood of graduating with a regular diploma' (abstract, conclusion) — the authors themselves call it exploratory; only 2 of 16 regular-diploma cells are significant (OR 1.464 at p < .1; OR 1.792 at p < .05), the estimates vanish under CEM with student controls, samples are 845–1,383 with unreconciled Ns, the treatment partly measures persistence, the modified diploma mechanically implies fewer core credits, and Appendix A7 shows no effect on graduating when diploma types are pooled. The defensible version is 'suggestive matched-comparison evidence of a shift from the modified toward the regular diploma, with no detectable effect on graduating overall.'

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The count is wrong. Under Table 8's own legend (** p < .05, * p < .1), seven of the sixteen regular-diploma cells are starred: for four-year core credits 1.425**, 1.48* and 1.464*; for five-year any credits 1.697**, 1.774** and 1.792**; and for five-year core credits 1.814**. Every star is consistent with its standard error. In the preferred Matching 3 column two of four cells are starred (1.464, p = .059; 1.792, p = .017). Supplemental Appendix A7 confirms no effect when regular and modified diplomas are pooled, and all eight modified-diploma cells are significant, so the abstract's claim survives in weakened form as a shift from modified to regular diplomas. On the sample sizes, Supplemental Table A2 gives matched Ns of 1,544, 1,502 and 1,024; Table 8's Ns are 71–90% of these and undocumented, and the text's 77%/72% retention rates match nothing. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table and the supplement.

- 'Extra time increased credit enrollment across all content areas and the likelihood of a full course load' (Table 6) — the subject outcomes are components of the treatment (coefficients sum to ~0.9), and the full-load odds ratios (1.996, 1.597) are mechanical and estimated on switchers only. Read Table 6 as an allocation table, not as causal effects.
- 'Extra instructional time' as a treatment comparable to extended-day, summer, or tutoring programs — it is a credit differential relative to non-EL peers, and the Discussion concedes most of it is probably fuller schedules or possibly repeated coursework (enrolled credits are not earned credits). Do not cite alongside program evaluations as though it estimates the same parameter.
- 'Extra time is concentrated in grades 11–12, suggesting it is used to support graduation' — 12th graders carry the fewest total and core credits of any grade; the flag rises because non-EL seniors drop to partial schedules, and the grade-12 surplus is entirely non-core.
- 'Extra time is distributed progressively to newcomers, long-term ELs, and ELs with disabilities' (Discussion, Conclusion) — holds only for the 'any' definition. For core content, dually identified students have 25% lower odds (OR 0.751) and a negative credit differential, long-term ELs are not different in the 'any' model, higher English proficiency predicts more core extra time, and the dominant gradient is grade level, not need. Table 3 also has no school fixed effects, so race/home-language contrasts may reflect which schools students attend.
- 'Longer school days served as the primary mechanism' (86%) — a residual category assigned whenever summer, online, or concurrent enrollment is not detected; definitional, not observed.
- 'Roughly one in five EL-classified students received extra time' — the figure is 18% of student-years, the Discussion says 'fewer than one in five,' and the paper never explains how a student with extra time in one of several observed years is classified.
- Every number in the graduation paragraph on p. 32 — 'OR = 0.0464' is 0.464 in Table 8; '88% lower' for OR 0.175 should be 82.5%; the continued panel headed 'Four-year outcomes' reports five-year core results; and Table 8's stars follow a convention (up to four asterisks) that appears nowhere else and is never defined.
- The 55% 'supplemental' and 32% 'displacement' figures — the Method defines displacement as lacking one or more of four core classes, the Findings as never enrolling in any of the four; the two rules cannot both yield 32%, and the tabulation is online-only (Appendix A6).
- The achievement null as a clean zero — classical measurement error in a peer-mean regressor is amplified by within-student differencing; the panel drops students on reclassification, which Appendix A3 suggests extra core time may cause; the treatment includes repeated failed courses; and the z-score standardization reference (statewide vs. within-EL) is stated only in an unseen appendix. Also note the effective identifying sample is far smaller than the printed Ns (only 52% of students have multiple observations; tested grades are 6, 7, 8, 11) and that the text's '0.010' for the 'any' ELA effect is 0.012 in Table 7.
- Table 1's graduation rows (4-year 0.20, 5-year 0.15, regular diploma 0.16) — computed over the full grades 6–12 panel, internally impossible as cumulative rates, and unrelated to the 68% state EL graduation rate cited on p. 8.
- Significance stars anywhere in the paper — a single asterisk means p < .05 in Table 5, p < .001 in Table 6, and p < .1 in Table 7; Tables 3 and 8 have no legend. Read magnitudes and check each table's note.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns.*

- External validity — one state, pre-COVID, 72% Latine and Spanish-speaking, 67% of districts under 5% EL, and a graduation finding that turns on Oregon's modified diploma (created 2009) with no direct analogue in most states. The treatment definition also depends on Oregon's 24-credit structure and on non-EL seniors reducing loads; do not assume replication elsewhere.
- The literature framing that 'research consistently has shown that increasing instructional time improves academic outcomes' and that prior work is 'predominantly small-scale' — the paper's own anchor (Kraft & Novicoff, 2024) is more cautious, and it omits the large-scale economics-of-time studies, the Chicago double-dose follow-up on course failure, the on-track/credit-accumulation literature, and the credit-recovery literature whose central caution (credentials rise without learning) is exactly the pattern this paper reports. 'ELD crowd out' is this team's own construct, not yet independently replicated.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper pairs excellent statewide administrative data with a genuinely novel, transparently constructed measure of instructional time, and the descriptive core (RQ1) is credible and well-executed. The causal claims (RQ2) are considerably weaker than the abstract implies: the course-taking 'effects' in Table 6 are largely an accounting decomposition of the treatment variable itself, and the graduation estimates in Table 8 are small-sample, threshold-dependent, and vulnerable to reverse causality through persistence and diploma-track circularity. The near-null achievement result is the most defensible causal-ish finding, though it too is attenuated by measurement error and treatment-induced sample attrition.

**Strengths:**

- Data are strong and appropriate for the question: the full Oregon student-level administrative panel of EL-classified students in grades 6-12, 2013-14 through 2018-19 (32,673 students; 64,162 student-year observations), with NCES SCED-coded course enrollment records that permit credit-level measurement of what students actually took, subject by subject.
- The core measurement innovation is well-motivated and clearly specified: instructional time is benchmarked against the mean enrolled credits of non-EL peers in the same grade x school x year, which differences out school scheduling norms, grade-level credit conventions, and year-to-year policy shifts, and does so without requiring the researchers to identify a named program. The 0.5-credit (one semester course) binary threshold is defended on interpretable grounds.
- The fixed-effects specification for RQ2 (Equation 3) is a sensible workhorse for this setting and is built up transparently across three models: student FE only (Model 1), plus grade-by-year and school FE and time-varying student characteristics (Model 2), plus time-varying instructional experiences (Model 3). Readers can see exactly how much of each estimate survives the added structure, which is where most of the informational value lies.
- The authors are unusually candid about the construct-validity problem at the heart of their own treatment. The Discussion section 'Supplemental Supports? Fuller Schedules? Repeated Coursework?' states plainly that much of what is flagged as 'extra' time is probably a fuller schedule rather than supplemental programming, and Limitations concedes that enrolled credits are not earned credits, so course repetition cannot be distinguished from supplementation.
- Data-quality claims are grounded rather than asserted: the authors report participant checks with state and district leaders about summer and online course under-reporting, and they correctly label the format tabulations in Table 4 as lower bounds.
- The handling of reclassification is thoughtful. The authors explicitly refuse to match on post-ninth-grade reclassification because it is post-treatment, and they report a supplementary CEM analysis (Appendix A3) suggesting extra core-content time may itself raise reclassification odds - while flagging the reverse interpretation. That is exactly the right instinct about a mediator.
- Failed approaches are disclosed rather than buried: generalized propensity-score and inverse-probability-weighting methods for the continuous treatment were attempted, did not balance, and are reported in Appendix A5 with the reason for not featuring them.
- The achievement effect size is interpreted honestly against Kraft's (2020) benchmarks and correctly characterized as below policy relevance rather than spun as a positive finding.

**Weaknesses:**

- The treatment is relative, not absolute, and the paper's own tables show the two can diverge sharply. In Table 2, 12th graders have the LOWEST total enrolled credits of any grade (6.11) and the lowest core credits (3.17), yet the highest share flagged as receiving extra time (53% any) and the largest average credit surplus (+0.31). The flag is being driven by non-EL seniors reducing their loads (early release, requirements met early), not by EL students receiving more instruction. The Table 3 grade coefficients confirm this: grade 12 is +0.384*** in the 'any' credit model but -0.031 (n.s.) in the 'core' credit model, and grade 11 is +0.184*** for any but -0.170*** for core. The extra time concentrated in the upper grades is essentially all non-core.
- The 'longer school day' format in Table 4 is defined residually - as more credits than the peer mean with none of the other formats observed - so the finding that 86% of extra time comes through a longer day is definitionally guaranteed by the treatment definition rather than measured. It is not evidence that schools lengthened the day for these students.
- Table 6 is largely a mechanical decomposition, not a set of causal effects. The outcomes (credits in ELA, math, science, social studies, ELD, electives) are the components that sum to the total credits from which the treatment variable is constructed. The Model 3 coefficients sum to 0.883 in middle school and 0.948 in high school - close to the 1.0 that arithmetic requires. A one-credit increase in the differential MUST be distributed across subjects. The authors recognize this circularity for the 'core' treatment (and correctly drop it for course-taking outcomes) but the same logic applies to the 'any' treatment.
- The full-course-load logit results are both mechanical and estimated on a heavily selected subsample. More total credits mechanically raises the odds of having all four core classes. And the FE logit uses only students whose full-load status changes: 4,857 of 26,461 middle school student-years and 5,007 of 12,104 high school student-years. The ORs of 1.996 and 1.597 are within-switcher estimates, not population effects.
- The graduation treatment - receiving extra time in at least 2 years of high school - is partly a proxy for staying enrolled. A student who leaves after 10th grade cannot accumulate two treated years; a student enrolled for four or five years has more chances to be flagged, including through summer courses. Since persistence is close to a prerequisite for graduation, this alone could generate positive regular-diploma odds. CEM matches only on ninth-grade-entry covariates (special education, newcomer, FRPL, cohort, gender, race/ethnicity, prior math and reading proficiency levels, ELP quintile), none of which capture subsequent persistence.
- The diploma-type results are potentially circular. Oregon's modified diploma has fewer core content requirements and fewer credit requirements. Being placed on the regular-diploma track therefore mechanically implies more core credits, which is what the 'core extra time' treatment measures. The strong negative modified-diploma odds (0.464 at 4 years, 0.175 at 5 years) paired with weaker positive regular-diploma odds and a null on any diploma (Appendix A7) is exactly the pattern one expects if the estimate is tracking diploma-track assignment rather than causing attainment.
- Table 8's estimates are non-monotone across specifications in a way that undermines them. For every outcome, adding CEM plus student controls (Matching 1) collapses the estimate toward 1 - 4-year regular any: 1.204 to 1.029; core: 1.425** to 1.244 n.s.; 5-year any: 1.697** to 1.111 n.s.; 5-year core: 1.814** to 1.285 n.s. - and then adding school and cohort fixed effects (Matching 2/3) restores it, often above the unmatched value (5-year any goes to 1.792**). In logit models with many school dummies and roughly 800-1,400 observations, this is a live incidental-parameters concern, not a sign the FE are cleaning up confounding.
- The graduation sample is small and shrinks further without explanation. The stated matched sample retains 77% (any) and 72% (core) of N = 2,130, yet Table 8 reports 1,383 / 1,338 for 4-year regular diploma, 1,259 / 1,136 for 4-year modified, and 882 / 845 and 767 / 730 for the 5-year models. The 5-year shrinkage is partly cohort truncation (only the 2013 and 2014 cohorts have observable 5-year outcomes by 2018-19), but the regular-versus-modified gap within the same 4-year window points to school-FE separation drops, which are non-random.
- The 2-or-more-years treatment threshold was chosen after continuous-treatment methods failed to balance, and no sensitivity to alternative thresholds (1 year, 3 years) is reported. Combined with 32 cells in Table 8 and no multiple-comparison adjustment, the two headline positive results (1.464 at p < .1 and 1.792 at p < .05) are thin.
- Sample selection in the main panel is endogenous to treatment. Students exit once reclassified, and the paper's own Appendix A3 suggests extra core-content time may increase reclassification. Students who received extra core time and gained most in English are therefore differentially removed from the achievement panel, biasing the achievement estimates toward zero. This is never discussed. Relatedly, only 52% of students have more than one observation, so the reported achievement Ns (27,476 for ELA; 27,336 for math) substantially overstate the effectively identifying sample, and the achievement models rely on grades 6, 7, 8, and 11 only - so most identification comes from 6-to-7 and 7-to-8 transitions.
- Clustering is inconsistent and probably too narrow in the causal models. Equations 1-2 cluster at the school level, but Equation 3 clusters at the student level even though the treatment is constructed from school x grade x year peer means and is plausibly driven by school-level scheduling decisions. The graduation models use robust (unclustered) standard errors despite school fixed effects. Several Table 7 and Table 8 estimates sit near conventional thresholds, so this matters.
- Model 3 controls include plausible mediators and post-treatment variables - whether ELD was integrated into a core class versus stand-alone (which directly determines credit counts and course access), whether the student had an ESL/bilingual-endorsed teacher (which depends on which courses the student is enrolled in), and, in the graduation model, whether the student ever waived EL services in high school. Conditioning on these can induce bias of unknown sign. In practice Models 2 and 3 barely differ, so this is a conceptual rather than quantitative problem here.
- Equation 1's subgroup logits have no school fixed effects, only school-clustered standard errors, even though 'extra time' is defined relative to same-school peers. Contrasts like Asian/Pacific Islander versus White (OR 1.314 for core) or Chinese versus Spanish home language (OR 0.557 for core) may reflect which schools and districts those students attend rather than differential within-school allocation.
- Unexplained sample and reporting discrepancies. The Data section reports 32,673 students and 64,162 observations; Tables 1 and 2 report 32,685 and 64,241. Table 3 reports N = 53,311 for all four models, roughly 17% below the panel, with no listwise-deletion explanation - and this is hard to reconcile with math and reading achievement being missing for 56-57% of student-years (Table 1) while Table 3 uses continuous math and reading z-scores as predictors. Table 1's graduation rows (4-year rate 0.20, 5-year rate 0.15, both lower than the 5-year rate should be if cumulative) are computed over the full grades 6-12 panel and bear no relation to Oregon's 68% EL graduation rate cited on page 8.
- Several small numerical and labeling errors that readers will trip on: the text reports 'OR = 0.0464' where Table 8 shows 0.464; it describes OR = 0.175 as '88% lower' when it is 82.5% lower; Table 1 prints '0.o6' for 0.06; the continued panel of Table 8 is headed 'Four-year outcomes' but reports the five-year core results (N = 845 / 730); and the star ladders differ across tables (Table 6: * = p < .001; Table 7: * = p < .1, ** = p < .01, *** = p < .001; Table 8 appears to use four levels), which invites misreading.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the treatment variable as 'enrolled in more credits than same-school, same-grade, same-year non-EL peers,' not as 'received supplemental instruction.' Anywhere the paper says extra instructional time, substitute that phrase and check whether the claim still reads the way you thought. The authors themselves make this concession in the Discussion; it should govern your reading of the whole paper.
- Do not read Table 4 as evidence that schools lengthened the day for EL students. 'Longer school day' is a residual category - it means 'above the peer mean and none of the other three formats were detected' - so the 86% figure is definitional, not measured. The informative content of Table 4 is the low end: summer (5%), online (1.4%), concurrent enrollment (3.2%), all acknowledged lower bounds.
- Treat the finding that extra time concentrates in grades 11-12 as most likely an artifact of the comparison group, not evidence that schools deploy extra time to support graduation. Table 2 shows 12th graders take the fewest total (6.11) and core (3.17) credits of any grade while being most often flagged; Table 3 shows the grade-12 surplus is entirely non-core (+0.384*** any versus -0.031 n.s. core). The pattern is consistent with non-EL seniors dropping to partial schedules.
- Read Table 6 as an allocation decomposition, not as causal effects. The coefficients sum to roughly 1 by construction (0.883 middle school, 0.948 high school, Model 3). What is genuinely informative is the SHARE of each marginal credit that lands where: about 45-48% goes to electives, 37-43% to the four core areas combined, 7-13% to ELD. That share finding is robust and is the paper's real contribution here. The framing of these numbers as 'estimated impacts' is not supportable.
- Discount the full-course-load odds ratios (1.996 middle school, 1.597 high school) on two grounds: taking more credits mechanically raises the chance of holding all four core classes, and the FE logit is estimated only on students who switch full-load status (4,857 of 26,461 and 5,007 of 12,104 student-years). Do not read these as population effects, and be skeptical of the abstract's claim that extra time 'substantially increased the likelihood of enrolling in a full course load.'
- The achievement nulls in Table 7 are the most trustworthy causal-flavored result in the paper, but interpret them as an upper bound on detectability rather than a clean zero. The one surviving estimate - 0.022 SD on ELA from the core credit differential, p < .01 - is correctly described by the authors as below policy relevance. Note also how fragile the larger Model 1 estimates are: ELA (any) falls from 0.028*** to 0.012 n.s. and math (core) from 0.023** to 0.010 n.s. once grade-by-year and school FE enter, meaning the raw associations were substantially driven by grade and cohort composition.
- When weighing the achievement null, factor in three forces that all push toward zero: classical measurement error in a peer-mean-based regressor is amplified by within-student differencing; the panel drops students the moment they reclassify, and the authors' own Appendix A3 suggests extra core time may cause reclassification, so the students who benefited most are differentially removed; and enrolled credits include repeated failed courses, diluting the treatment. A modest true effect could be masked. 'No large positive achievement effect detected' is the defensible reading; 'extra time does not improve achievement' is not.
- Treat every graduation estimate in Table 8 as exploratory - the authors say so explicitly, and the table supports that caution more than the abstract does. In particular, note that CEM plus student controls (Matching 1) wipes out the effect in all four regular-diploma rows, and only the addition of school and cohort fixed effects to samples of 845-1,383 observations restores it. The two significant regular-diploma results (OR 1.464 at p < .1 for 4-year core; OR 1.792 at p < .05 for 5-year any) are 2 of 16 cells with no multiple-comparison adjustment and a post hoc treatment threshold.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The count is wrong. Under Table 8's own legend (** p < .05, * p < .1), seven of the sixteen regular-diploma cells are starred: for four-year core credits 1.425**, 1.48* and 1.464*; for five-year any credits 1.697**, 1.774** and 1.792**; and for five-year core credits 1.814**. Every star is consistent with its standard error. In the preferred Matching 3 column two of four cells are starred (1.464, p = .059; 1.792, p = .017). Supplemental Appendix A7 confirms no effect when regular and modified diplomas are pooled, and all eight modified-diploma cells are significant, so the abstract's claim survives in weakened form as a shift from modified to regular diplomas. On the sample sizes, Supplemental Table A2 gives matched Ns of 1,544, 1,502 and 1,024; Table 8's Ns are 71–90% of these and undocumented, and the text's 77%/72% retention rates match nothing. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table and the supplement.

- Before citing the graduation result, ask whether the treatment is measuring persistence. 'Extra time in at least 2 years of high school' cannot be earned by a student who leaves early, and matching is on ninth-grade-entry covariates only. The regular-diploma odds ratios may substantially reflect that treated students were still enrolled, which is close to tautological for graduation.
- Read the diploma-type contrast with the circularity in mind: Oregon's modified diploma requires less core content, so being on the regular-diploma track mechanically produces more core credits, which is the treatment. The pattern of strong negative modified-diploma odds, weaker positive regular-diploma odds, and a null on any diploma (Appendix A7) is what you would see if the estimate captures track assignment rather than causing attainment. The substantively interesting version of this claim - that extra time moves students off the modified-diploma pathway - is the one most exposed to this problem.
- Read Table 3's subgroup contrasts as descriptions of which EL students carry heavier loads relative to their non-EL schoolmates, not as evidence of within-school differential allocation. Equation 1 has no school fixed effects, so between-school sorting is embedded in the race/ethnicity and home-language coefficients. The paper's own summary of Table 3's intercepts also over-reads them: an intercept of -0.280 is the value for the reference student (developmental EL, White, Spanish home language, grade 9, mean z-scores), not a population baseline. The sample-average deficits in Table 2 (-0.02 any, -0.21 core) are the number to cite.
- Table 5's near-universal p < .001 stars reflect the panel's size (64,241 student-years, students appearing repeatedly, no clustering adjustment, ~42 comparisons), not effect magnitude. Read the credit differences instead. The substantive story is the ratio: among EL students with extra time, the surplus is +0.61 elective credits versus +0.07 ELA, +0.03 math, +0.02 science, +0.11 social studies, +0.11 ELD - and these sum to roughly the 0.95-credit differential by construction.
- Do not read Table 1's graduation rows (4-year rate 0.20, 5-year 0.15) as EL graduation rates. They are computed over the entire grades 6-12 student-year panel, most of whom are not in a graduation cohort, and they are internally odd (a 5-year rate below the 4-year rate). Use the state figures on page 8 (68% for current ELs) or the separate N = 2,130 graduation sample for that purpose.
- Bound the external validity tightly. This is one state, pre-COVID (2013-14 through 2018-19), with an EL population that is 72% Latine and 72% Spanish-speaking. The graduation finding turns on Oregon's modified diploma, which has no direct analogue in most states, and the treatment definition depends on Oregon's 24-credit / six-credits-per-year structure and on the local norm of non-EL seniors reducing loads. Replication elsewhere should not be assumed.
- Verify against the online appendix before building on the graduation results specifically: Table A2 (CEM covariate balance before and after matching, and who the 23-28% pruned students were), Table A5 (the IPW estimates the authors decline to discuss), Table A3 (the reclassification models), and Table A7 (the any-diploma null). The paper's most-quoted claim rests on material the printed article does not show.
- Note the reporting slips when quoting numbers: the text's 'OR = 0.0464' should be 0.464; 'OR = 0.175' is 82.5% lower, not 88%; and the continued panel of Table 8 labeled 'Four-year outcomes' (N = 845 / 730) actually reports five-year core results. Significance ladders also differ across tables - in Table 7 a single asterisk is p < .1, in Table 6 it is p < .001.

**Detailed Commentary:**

OVERALL POSITION

This is a well-resourced, competently executed study whose descriptive contribution is considerably more solid than its causal contribution, and whose abstract and conclusion promise more causal weight than Tables 6-8 can carry. The measurement innovation is genuinely useful and the authors are refreshingly candid about several of its problems. But two structural issues - the mechanical relationship between the treatment and the course-taking outcomes, and the reverse-causality/circularity problems in the graduation design - are not adequately confronted, and they sit underneath the two claims the abstract leads with. 'Adequate' rather than 'strong' reflects that gap between what the design supports and what the paper headlines; it is not a judgment that the work is poorly done.

1. THE TREATMENT VARIABLE (pp. 12-13)

Extra instructional time is defined as a student's total enrolled credits minus the mean enrolled credits of all non-EL peers in the same grade, school, and year, with a binary flag at +0.5 credits (one semester course). Two versions exist: 'any' (all subjects) and 'core' (ELA, math, science, social studies). Credits follow Oregon's convention where a year-long course is 1.0, and a student counts as enrolled only if enrolled for more than 50% of the course's duration - a sensible guard against transfer artifacts.

The design virtue is real: differencing against same-school, same-grade, same-year non-EL peers removes school scheduling norms, grade-level credit conventions, and statewide policy shifts without requiring the researchers to name a program. Prior work in this area is almost entirely single-program evaluation, and this is a defensible way to get statewide coverage.

The cost is construct validity, and it is larger than the paper's framing admits. Being 0.5 credits above the non-EL mean is not the same as receiving supplemental instruction. It can equally mean the student holds an ordinary full schedule while the comparison group has partially emptied theirs. The paper's own numbers make this concrete. In Table 2, 12th graders take the FEWEST total credits of any grade (6.11 versus 6.73-7.02 in grades 6-11) and the fewest core credits (3.17 versus 3.39-4.07), yet 53% are flagged as receiving extra time (any) - triple the grade 6-10 rates - with the largest average surplus (+0.31). The Table 3 grade coefficients pin down the mechanism: grade 12 relative to grade 9 is OR 9.351*** in the 'any' extra-time logit and +0.384*** in the 'any' credit model, but only 2.193*** and -0.031 (n.s.) in the core models; grade 11 is +0.184*** for any and -0.170*** for core. The upper-grade surplus is entirely non-core, and it appears precisely where non-EL seniors would be dropping to partial schedules. The Discussion (p. 33) concedes this - 'we suspect that many students that we identified as receiving "extra" instruction simply had fuller high school schedules' - but the abstract, the finding that extra time is 'concentrated in the last 2 years of high school, suggesting that it is being used as a tool to support graduation' (p. 33), and the conclusion do not carry the concession forward.

A second measurement issue the paper does not raise: no minimum cell size is stated for the non-EL peer mean. In schools or grade cells with few non-EL students, the benchmark is noisy, and that noise enters the treatment. In a within-student fixed-effects model, classical measurement error in the regressor is amplified by differencing, attenuating estimates toward zero. This matters directly for reading Table 7.

Third, enrolled credits are not earned credits (Limitations, p. 36). A student repeating a failed course is coded identically to a student receiving supplemental support. Given the literature the paper itself reviews - extra time typically follows course failure (Heinrich & Darling-Aduana, 2021; Vandell et al., 2007) - a nontrivial share of the treated population is likely negatively selected on unmeasured contemporaneous struggle.

2. RQ1 DESCRIPTIVE RESULTS (Tables 2-5)

The headline descriptive finding - EL-classified students on average take 0.21 FEWER core credits and 0.02 fewer total credits than same-school, same-grade, same-year non-EL peers, with only 17-18% of student-years above the +0.5 threshold (Table 2) - is the most trustworthy result in the paper. It is a transparent arithmetic comparison on administrative data, it replicates the authors' prior multistate work (Umansky et al., 2024), and no modeling choices intervene. Readers can rely on it, and on the associated point that the deficit is deepest for the lowest-proficiency students (ELP-beginning: -0.29 any, -0.76 core, Table 2).

Table 4 (formats) should be read with care. 'Longer school day' is defined in the table note as more credits than the peer mean AND none of the other three formats detected. That is a residual bucket, definitionally coextensive with the treatment. The 86% (any) and 65% (core) figures therefore cannot be evidence that schools extended the day; they are what is left after summer (5.0% / 2.4%), online (1.4% / 1.0%), and concurrent enrollment (3.2% / 1.5%) are subtracted - all of which the authors correctly flag as under-reported lower bounds. The right reading of Table 4 is that identifiable alternative delivery formats are rare in these data, and that the residual is uninterpretable as a mechanism.

Table 5 is an allocation decomposition. Comparing EL students with and without extra time by subject and grade, the total-row differences are +0.07 ELA, +0.03 math, +0.02 science, +0.11 social studies, +0.11 ELD, +0.61 electives - summing to about 0.95, essentially the 0.96-credit 'any' differential reported in the text (p. 19). This is arithmetic, not a comparison of comparable students. The informative content is the composition: roughly two-thirds of the surplus goes to electives. Note footnote 3's important caveat that Oregon's 'electives' category here includes graduation-required world languages, financial education, PE, health, and arts/CTE, so the elective share is not straightforwardly wasted time. The t-tests attached to Table 5 are essentially uninformative: with 64,241 student-year observations, repeated observations per student, no clustering adjustment, and roughly 42 comparisons, nearly everything is p < .001. Read magnitudes only.

Table 3's subgroup models (Equations 1-2) are pooled logit and OLS with school-clustered standard errors but NO school fixed effects. Since 'extra time' is defined relative to same-school peers, contrasts across race/ethnicity and home language - Asian/Pacific Islander OR 1.314** for core, Chinese home language OR 0.557** for core, Vietnamese OR 0.587* - may be reflecting which schools and districts those groups attend rather than within-school allocation decisions. Given the paper's framing around equity in allocation, this is a meaningful limitation. The text also over-reads the intercepts: the claim that 'EL-classified students overall enrolled in significantly less total instructional time than their non-EL peers, reflected in the -0.28 intercept' (p. 19) misinterprets a reference-category value (developmental EL, White, Spanish home language, grade 9, not dually identified, not economically disadvantaged, mean z-scores) as a population mean. The substantive claim is correct, but Table 2's raw means are the right support for it, not the intercept.

Table 3 also reports N = 53,311 for all four models, about 17% below the 64,241-observation panel, with no explanation. This is hard to square with Table 1's report that math and reading achievement are missing for 56-57% of student-years while Table 3 uses continuous math and reading z-scores as predictors - presumably the authors carry forward the most recent available prior score, but this is not documented, and it is a genuine reproducibility gap.

3. THE FIXED-EFFECTS COURSE-TAKING MODELS (Table 6)

Equation 3 includes student, grade-by-year, and school fixed effects, time-varying student characteristics, and time-varying instructional experiences, with student-clustered standard errors. As a design for absorbing time-invariant student heterogeneity this is appropriate and the model build-up (Models 1-3) is transparent.

The problem is that the outcomes are components of the treatment. TIME(any) = total credits minus the non-EL peer mean, and total credits = ELA + math + science + social studies + ELD + electives. Regressing each subject's credits on the total differential is therefore a decomposition of where a marginal credit lands. The Model 3 coefficients bear this out: middle school 0.108 + 0.104 + 0.054 + 0.101 + 0.397 + 0.119 = 0.883; high school 0.119 + 0.115 + 0.108 + 0.088 + 0.452 + 0.066 = 0.948. Both approach the 1.0 that the accounting identity requires (deviations reflect the fixed effects and the varying peer-mean term). The authors recognize the circularity for the 'core' treatment and explicitly drop it for course-taking outcomes ('there is a circular causal relationship between being enrolled in more core credits and having higher credits in core classes,' p. 16), but the same logic applies to 'any' - it is just spread across six outcomes rather than concentrated in one. Describing this as 'a positive estimated impact on credit enrollment across all content areas' (p. 25) and as 'sizable and positive effects' (p. 27) overstates it. What is genuinely informative and worth citing is the SHARE structure: electives absorb 45% (MS) to 48% (HS) of each marginal credit, the four core areas together absorb 42% (MS, 0.367) to 45% (HS, 0.430), and ELD absorbs 13% (MS) to 7% (HS).

The full-academic-load logit ORs (1.996 MS, 1.597 HS) compound two problems. First, they are close to mechanical: 'full load' means enrolled in all four core content areas, and more total credits mechanically raises that probability. Second, the note under Table 6 discloses that the FE logit uses only students whose full-load status changes: 4,857 of 26,461 middle school student-years and 5,007 of 12,104 high school student-years. That is a within-switcher estimand, and switchers are not a random subset of the panel. The abstract's claim that extra time 'substantially increased the likelihood of their enrolling in a full course load' should be read with both discounts applied.

4. THE ACHIEVEMENT MODELS (Table 7)

These are the paper's most defensible causal-flavored estimates, and their near-null character is credible. Note first how much the estimates move as structure is added: ELA (any) 0.028*** to 0.011 to 0.012 (n.s.); ELA (core) 0.036*** to 0.022** to 0.022**; math (any) 0.014* to 0.003 to 0.002; math (core) 0.023** to 0.010 to 0.010. Roughly half to all of each Model 1 estimate is grade-by-year and school composition. Only ELA (core) survives, at 0.022 SD, which the authors correctly characterize against Kraft (2020) as very small and below policy relevance. (Note Table 7's unusual star ladder: * = p < .1, ** = p < .01, *** = p < .001, skipping .05.)

Three things should temper the reading in the direction of 'undetected' rather than 'absent.' First, measurement error in the peer-mean-benchmarked treatment is amplified by within-student differencing, attenuating toward zero. Second - and this is not discussed anywhere in the paper - the panel is restricted to CURRENTLY classified ELs, so students exit the moment they reclassify (p. 9, footnote 2). The authors' own Appendix A3 analysis suggests extra core-content time may INCREASE reclassification odds. That makes attrition from the panel a downstream consequence of treatment, and it removes disproportionately the students for whom extra time worked best in English. Third, the treatment includes repeated failed coursework, diluting the intended dose.

Working against those: the within-student identification is off year-to-year changes in the credit differential, and the plausible drivers of such changes - course failure triggering recovery enrollment, a counselor intervening after a bad year - are correlated with contemporaneous achievement shocks. The paper names this as 'the main threat to causal inference' (p. 17) but does not test it. The standard diagnostics are absent: no lead-lag or event-study specification showing that future credit differentials do not predict current test scores, no pre-trend check. Given the design, that omission is the largest missed opportunity in the paper.

Also note the achievement panel uses only grades 6, 7, 8, and 11 (the tested grades), so with student fixed effects, identification comes overwhelmingly from 6-to-7 and 7-to-8 transitions, with 8-to-11 transitions rare in a panel where only 52% of students have more than one observation at all. The reported N = 27,476 (ELA) and 27,336 (math) overstate the effectively identifying sample by a wide margin. The estimate is also contemporaneous - same-year credit differential on same-year spring test score - so it is a within-year dose response, not a cumulative-exposure effect. No lagged or cumulative specification is presented.

Finally, standard errors are clustered at the student level while the treatment derives from school x grade x year peer means and is plausibly determined by school scheduling decisions. School-level clustering (as used in Equations 1-2) would be more defensible and would widen the intervals. Since ELA (core) at 0.022 with SE 0.008 is the only surviving result, this is not merely pedantic.

5. THE GRADUATION MODELS (Table 8) - THE FRAGILE CORE

This is where reader caution should be greatest, and where the gap between the abstract ('substantially increased the likelihood of ... graduating with a regular diploma') and the evidence is widest. The authors themselves call these results 'exploratory' (p. 29) and 'tentative causal estimates' (p. 18); readers should take that at face value.

Sample and design. N = 2,130 students classified as ELs at ninth-grade entry in the 2013-16 cohorts, collapsed to one observation each. CEM requires exact matches on special education status, newcomer status, FRPL, cohort, gender, race/ethnicity, and prior math and reading proficiency levels (missing as a category), plus quintile matching on ELP scale scores; 77% (any) / 72% (core) of the sample is retained. The treatment - extra time in at least 2 years of high school - was chosen after generalized propensity-score and IPW approaches for the continuous treatment failed to balance (p. 17). Models are logit with school and cohort fixed effects and robust standard errors, weighted by CEM weights, with matching variables re-entered as controls (the 'doubly robust' claim).

Reverse causality through persistence. This is the most serious unaddressed threat. Accumulating two treated years requires being enrolled for at least two years; a student who leaves after 10th grade cannot be treated. Since remaining enrolled is close to a precondition for graduating, the treatment partially encodes the outcome. Nothing in the matching set - all ninth-grade-entry characteristics - captures subsequent persistence. This mechanism alone could produce the positive regular-diploma odds.

Diploma-track circularity. Oregon's modified diploma is defined by fewer core content requirements and less advanced content (pp. 8-9, 34-35). A student on the regular-diploma track therefore takes more core credits by definition, and 'extra core time' is precisely a measure of taking more core credits than peers. The strong modified-diploma results (OR 0.464, p < .01 at 4 years; OR 0.175, p < .001 at 5 years) combined with weaker regular-diploma results and, per Appendix A7, a NULL on any diploma, is exactly the signature of an estimate that tracks diploma-track assignment rather than causing attainment. The authors report the appendix null honestly but do not draw this inference.

Instability across specifications. Reading Table 8 column by column is deflating. Four-year regular diploma, any: 1.204 (no matching) to 1.029 (Matching 1) to 1.145 to 1.133 - never significant. Four-year regular, core: 1.425** to 1.244 (n.s.) to 1.48* to 1.464*. Five-year regular, any: 1.697** to 1.111 (n.s.) to 1.774** to 1.792**. Five-year regular, core: 1.814** to 1.285 (n.s.) to 1.52 (n.s.) to 1.488 (n.s.). In every single case, CEM plus student controls kills the effect, and adding school and cohort fixed effects revives it, often above the unmatched value. That non-monotonicity is not the signature of confounding being progressively removed. With 845-1,383 observations and a school dummy for every Oregon high school enrolling ninth-grade ELs, incidental-parameters bias in FE logit - which pushes estimates away from the null in short panels - is a live alternative explanation for the Matching 2/3 revival.

Sample attrition within Table 8. Against a matched base of roughly 1,640 (any) and 1,534 (core), the reported Ns are 1,383 / 1,338 (4-year regular), 1,259 / 1,136 (4-year modified), 882 / 845 and 767 / 730 (5-year). The 5-year shrinkage is largely cohort truncation - only the 2013 and 2014 cohorts have observable 5-year outcomes within the 2018-19 data window - but the 4-year regular-versus-modified gap within an identical sample points to school-FE separation drops, which discard exactly the schools with no outcome variation. The 5-year estimates in particular rest on roughly 40% of the matched sample.

Multiplicity and researcher degrees of freedom. Table 8 contains 32 estimates. The 2-or-more-years threshold was selected post hoc after a different estimator failed, and no alternative thresholds are shown. Only two regular-diploma cells reach any significance, one at p < .1. No adjustment for multiple comparisons is applied.

Inference. Robust but unclustered standard errors are used despite school fixed effects and school-level determination of scheduling. School clustering would widen the intervals for estimates already sitting near thresholds.

Reporting errors to note when quoting: the text gives 'OR = 0.0464' where Table 8 shows 0.464; describes OR = 0.175 as '88% lower' when it is 82.5% lower; and the continued panel of Table 8 is headed 'Four-year outcomes' while reporting five-year core results (N = 845 / 730). Table 8's star ladder appears to be * = p < .1, ** = p < .05, *** = p < .01, **** = p < .001, inferred from the text's parenthetical p-values rather than stated legibly in the extracted note.

6. WHAT I COULD NOT ASSESS

Appendix Tables A1-A7 are not in the printed article. Specifically unverifiable: A2 (CEM covariate balance before and after matching, and the characteristics of the 23-28% pruned - the paper asserts 'strong matches' but shows none); A5 (the IPW continuous-treatment results, dismissed 'due to poor matches,' so readers cannot see whether they contradict the CEM findings); A3 (the reclassification models, which bear directly on the endogenous-attrition problem in the achievement panel); A4 (the crosswalk between OAKS/Smarter Balanced and ELPA/ELPA21 across the assessment transitions, which underlies every z-score in Table 7); A6 (supplement-versus-displacement tabulations); and A7 (the any-diploma null). Anyone planning to build on the graduation result should read A2 and A5 first. This limits my confidence to 0.78.

7. BOTTOM LINE FOR READERS

Rely on: (a) the descriptive finding that EL-classified secondary students in Oregon enroll in fewer core credits than same-school, same-grade, same-year non-EL peers (-0.21 credits, Table 2); (b) the finding that only about 17-18% of EL student-years exceed the +0.5-credit threshold, given the peer-relative definition; (c) the allocation finding that when EL students do carry surplus credits, roughly two-thirds to nearly half of the surplus goes to electives rather than core content (Tables 5 and 6); and (d) the conclusion that no large positive achievement effect is detectable, with the caveat that several forces bias toward zero.

Treat cautiously: every estimate in Table 6 framed as an 'effect' (decomposition), the full-course-load odds ratios (mechanical plus movers-only), the claim that longer school days are the dominant delivery format (residual definition), the concentration of extra time in grades 11-12 as evidence of graduation strategy (comparison-group artifact), the Table 3 subgroup contrasts as within-school allocation (no school FE), and above all every graduation estimate in Table 8 (persistence-driven treatment, diploma-track circularity, small and unstable samples, post hoc threshold, unadjusted multiplicity). The paper's own limitations section and Discussion anticipate several of these; the abstract and conclusion do not.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The literature review is unusually well-organized — it mirrors the four research questions twice, once for the general student population and once for EL-classified students, which makes both the state of knowledge and the gap the paper fills easy to see — and it is genuinely interdisciplinary, drawing on sociology of education, developmental psychology, economics, and qualitative EL scholarship. But it under-engages three adjacent literatures that bear directly on its own results: the economics of instructional time beyond the handful of studies cited, the Chicago on-track/credit-accumulation research that underwrites its main outcome, and the credit-recovery evidence base whose central caution (graduation rates rise without learning rising) is precisely the pattern this paper reports. Readers should treat the review as an honest and well-structured map of the EL-specific literature, which really is thin, and as an incomplete map of the general instructional-time and credit-accumulation literatures.

**Strengths:**

- The review's architecture is a model of transparency: it walks through who gets extra time, how they get it, what it is used for, and what its effects are — first for students generally, then for EL-classified students — so the reader can see exactly which cells of that grid are empty in the EL literature. Very few papers make their own contribution this legible.
- It is honest about the weakness of the EL-specific evidence rather than inflating it. Arbreton et al. (2008) is explicitly flagged as lacking a comparison group; Farbman (2015), Matthews and Mellom (2012), Schneider (2020), and Lopez et al. (2020) are correctly characterized as small-scale, descriptive, or qualitative; and the retention studies (Figlio and Ozek, 2020; Quintero, 2024) are paired with the National Education Policy Center (2019) critique rather than presented as clean endorsements of retention.
- Genuinely interdisciplinary. Lareau (2011), Buchmann et al. (2010), and Snellman et al. (2015) supply the sociological framing of shadow education; Simpkins et al. (2011, 2017), Camacho and Fuligni (2015), Durlak et al. (2010), and Riggs et al. (2010) bring developmental psychology and out-of-school-time research; Cortes and Goodman (2014), Cortes et al. (2015), Figlio and Ozek (2020), Rivkin and Schiman (2015), and Cattaneo et al. (2017) bring economics. For an AERJ paper this breadth is above the norm.
- The review takes seriously the distinction between public/compensatory and private/enrichment extra time, and the resulting 'bifurcated distribution' claim is a useful analytic frame that the paper then tests empirically. This is a case where the literature review does real work rather than serving as decoration.
- The Discussion, not just the review, engages the paper's own inconvenient result. The near-zero achievement effects are read against Kraft and Novicoff's (2024) total-time / instructional-time / learning-time taxonomy, against the possibility that extra time went to electives, and against the measurement-validity literature on English-language standardized tests for EL students (Abedi, 2002; Witmer and Marinho, 2025). That is more self-critical engagement than most papers offer.
- Community-based and heritage-language education is acknowledged (Baldridge et al., 2017; Zhou and Li, 2003) rather than treated as outside the frame, and the limitations section explicitly names non-credit-bearing and community-based extra time as excluded. Readers get an accurate scope statement.

**Weaknesses:**

- The framing sentence 'Research consistently has shown that increasing instructional time improves academic outcomes' overstates the evidence base and is not what the paper's own anchor citation concludes. Kraft and Novicoff's (2024) synthesis emphasizes wide heterogeneity and that added school time frequently does not translate into added learning time. The extended-learning-time evaluation literature includes prominent null results, and the review gives those roughly one clause (Custers, 2025; Heinrich and Darling-Aduana, 2021; Rivkin and Schiman, 2015) against several sentences of affirmative framing.
- The economics-of-instructional-time literature is represented by a thin and somewhat idiosyncratic slice. Cattaneo et al. (2017), Rivkin and Schiman (2015), and Jez and Wassmer (2015) are cited, but the studies that use exactly this paper's identification logic — within-student variation in time across subjects or years — are absent. I am reasonably confident that Lavy's Economic Journal work on cross-national differences in instructional time and Taylor's Journal of Public Economics regression-discontinuity study of double-period middle school math both exist and are directly on point, as is Figlio, Holden, and Ozek's regression-discontinuity evaluation of Florida's mandated extra literacy hour — the last especially, since it is a statewide extended-day mandate in a heavily EL-serving state.
- The double-dose literature is cited only through the findings that support extra time. Cortes and Goodman (2014), Cortes et al. (2015), and Nomi and Allensworth (2009) are all there, but I am reasonably confident that Nomi and Allensworth also published a follow-up (in AERJ, around 2013) showing that Chicago's double-dose algebra raised test scores while increasing course failure and simultaneously producing ability sorting within schools. That finding cuts directly against this paper's story — more time in core content, small achievement gains, but a completion cost the paper explicitly cannot observe because Oregon's data do not record whether enrolled credits were earned.
- The credit-accumulation and on-track literature is essentially missing, even though 'enrollment in a full academic course load' and 'graduating with a regular diploma' are the paper's headline outcomes. The Chicago Consortium on School Research work by Allensworth and Easton establishing freshman-year credit accumulation and course failure as the dominant predictor of graduation is the natural theoretical bridge between this paper's course-taking findings and its graduation findings, and it does not appear. Royster et al. (2015) and Furstenberg and Neumark (2007) are gestured at in the Discussion but do not substitute.
- The credit-recovery literature is cited for its descriptive prevalence (U.S. Department of Education, 2018; Kuhfeld et al., 2025) and for its quality concerns (Darling-Aduana, 2021; Darling-Aduana et al., 2024; Heinrich and Darling-Aduana, 2021), but not for the interpretive problem it poses. The central finding of that literature is that credit recovery raises credit accumulation and graduation rates without commensurate gains in measured learning. That is exactly the result pattern this paper reports — large effects on full course load and regular-diploma receipt, near-zero effects on test scores — and the paper never confronts the possibility that its graduation effect is a credentialing effect rather than a learning effect. I am reasonably confident the Heppen et al. randomized trial of online versus face-to-face algebra credit recovery exists and belongs here, along with the policy commentary on credit recovery and graduation-rate inflation.
- The EL reclassification literature is barely engaged despite mattering to the design. The paper reports that 55 percent of its graduation sample reclassified during high school, explicitly declines to match on reclassification because it is post-treatment, and runs a supplementary analysis suggesting extra core-content time may increase reclassification. That is a substantial claim, and it is made without engaging the regression-discontinuity literature on the effects of EL reclassification on course access and attainment (work by, among others, Robinson-Cimpian and Thompson, Carlson and Knowles, Johnson, Pope, and Umansky) — literature the third author has contributed to.
- The author team's own prior work carries a disproportionate share of the theoretical load. 'ELD crowd out,' the construct that anchors the entire framing, rests on a single 2024 paper by the same authors (Umansky et al., 2024), which is cited at least six times, alongside Thompson et al. (2026), Bromley et al. (2025), Shin et al. (2026, a conference presentation), and Vazquez Cano et al. (2021). The self-citation is substantively defensible — this team is the leading source on secondary EL course access — but readers should know the construct has not yet been independently replicated. Notably, Umansky's own earlier and highly relevant AERJ work on leveled and exclusionary tracking for EL students (circa 2016) is not cited, nor is Callahan, Wilkinson, and Muller's work on ESL placement and course-taking, though Callahan (2005) is.
- Two concrete citation defects. First, Mulhern (2023) is cited in the Methods to justify the school-counselor full-time-equivalence covariate but has no entry in the reference list — this is almost certainly Mulhern's American Economic Review paper on individual school counselors' effects on educational attainment, but readers cannot verify it from the paper. Second, the in-text 'Kim, 2024' in the shadow-education passage corresponds to a reference-list entry authored by Kim, Goodman, and West (2024) and should be 'Kim et al., 2024'; anyone tracing that claim will look for the wrong paper.
- Several formatting and dating irregularities in the reference list suggest incomplete copyediting and are worth noticing before repeating any citation: 'Buchmann, et al, 2010' and 'Snellman, et al., 2015' carry stray commas in text; the Figlio and Ozek (2020) entry lists article number 104155 but a DOI ending in 104184; Quintero (2024) is styled as a November 2024 conference presentation but points to an Annenberg working-paper URL numbered ai25-1247, implying a 2025 paper; and the list is misalphabetized in several places (AASA before Abedi, Kim before Kieffer, Jimenez-Castellanos after Johnson).
- The summer-school and tutoring literatures are represented by one or two recent studies each rather than by their synthesis anchors. Callen et al. (2025) and Lynch et al. (2024) stand in for summer school, and Bennett et al. (2024) for tutoring. I am reasonably confident that Cooper and colleagues' meta-analysis of summer school, Kim and Quinn's Review of Educational Research meta-analysis of summer reading interventions, and Nickow, Oreopoulos, and Quan's meta-analysis of tutoring all exist and are the standard reference points a reader would expect. The practical stakes are modest here — summer accounts for only 5 percent of extra-time cases in the data — but the omissions make the affirmative framing of the time literature look better supported than it is.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read this paper for what it measures, not for what its title says. The construct is a credit-load differential relative to same-school, same-grade, same-year non-EL peers — not instructional hours, not a program. The authors themselves say in the Discussion that much of what they flag as 'extra time' is likely just a fuller schedule for students who could not afford to lighten their load. Cite this paper for statewide patterns in relative credit load among secondary EL students; do not cite it as an estimate of the effect of an extended-time intervention.
- Pair it with Kraft and Novicoff (2024) before drawing any 'more time works' conclusion. That synthesis is the paper's own anchor and is considerably more cautious than the paper's framing sentence; its total-time / instructional-time / learning-time distinction is the right lens for reading this paper's near-zero achievement estimates.
- For the interpretive question the paper leaves open — whether the graduation gain reflects learning or credentialing — go to the credit-recovery literature rather than to this paper. Heppen and colleagues' randomized trial of online versus face-to-face credit recovery, and the policy debate over credit recovery and graduation-rate inflation, supply the competing hypothesis: that credit accumulation and diploma receipt can move substantially while measured achievement does not. This paper's own limitation — Oregon data do not record whether enrolled credits were earned — makes that hypothesis unusually hard to rule out here.
- For the missing theoretical bridge between the course-taking results and the graduation results, read Allensworth and Easton's on-track indicator work from the Chicago Consortium. It establishes why credit accumulation and course failure in ninth grade predict graduation, and it is the framework that would make this paper's 'full course load' outcome interpretable as more than a mechanical consequence of enrolling in more classes.
- Before repeating the paper's characterization of the double-dose evidence, check Nomi and Allensworth's follow-up work on Chicago double-dose algebra (I believe an AERJ article around 2013). My recollection is that it documents increased course failure and within-school ability sorting alongside test-score gains — a counterweight this paper does not carry.
- Two citations in this paper are worth verifying before you repeat them. The sentence 'Two papers, by Figlio and Ozek (2020) and Quintero (2024), both found positive effects on EL students from state-level third grade retention policies in Florida and Texas' compresses two studies with important caveats about who is retained, the bundling of retention with instructional supports (which the paper does note), and possible fade-out; go to the originals. And 'Kim, 2024' should be read as Kim, Goodman, and West (2024) on private tutoring centers.
- Note that Mulhern (2023), cited in the Methods to justify the school-counselor covariate, is absent from the reference list. If the counselor control matters to your reading of the graduation models, you will need to locate the source yourself; the likely referent is Mulhern's American Economic Review paper on school counselor effects.
- Treat 'ELD crowd out' as a construct from this research team rather than as an established field-wide finding. It originates in Umansky et al. (2024), by the same authors, and has not yet been independently replicated. The empirical claim it rests on — that secondary EL students enroll in fewer core credits than peers — is corroborated here in Oregon, which strengthens it, but the corroboration is not independent.
- For the causal-inference antecedents at the secondary EL level, the closest prior work is Johnson (2020, AERJ) on summer credit recovery for newcomers, which the paper cites but does not position itself carefully against. Johnson already provides a quasi-experimental secondary-level estimate of one form of extra time on credit accumulation. This paper's novelty is scope — statewide, format-agnostic, all EL subgroups — not the fact of a causal estimate.
- If you are reading this alongside the economics literature on instructional time, supply the missing comparisons yourself: Lavy's cross-national work in the Economic Journal, Taylor's regression-discontinuity study of double-period math in the Journal of Public Economics, and Figlio, Holden, and Ozek's evaluation of Florida's mandated extra literacy hour. All three use large-scale designs that undercut the paper's framing that prior work has been 'predominantly small-scale interventions.'
- If your interest is reclassification, note that the supplementary finding that extra core-content time may raise reclassification likelihood (Appendix Table A3) is presented with an explicit and correct warning that reverse causality is possible. Read it against the regression-discontinuity reclassification literature — which this paper does not engage — before treating it as evidence about anything.

**Detailed Commentary:**

SCOPE AND STRUCTURE

The literature review runs roughly six journal pages and is built as a two-pass grid: four subheadings (who gets extra time, how they receive it, what it is used for, how it affects outcomes) applied first to the general student population and then to EL-classified students. This is an unusually disciplined structure and it pays off — it renders the paper's contribution claim almost self-evident, because the EL half of the grid is visibly emptier than the general half. Readers evaluating whether the gap is real should note that the structure itself does rhetorical work: by defining the grid, the authors also define what counts as a gap.

WHAT THE REVIEW COVERS WELL

The shadow-education and out-of-school-time strand is well handled. Buchmann, Condron, and Roscigno (2010), Snellman et al. (2015), Lareau (2011), and Kim, Goodman, and West (2024) supply the sociological account of privately purchased extra time; Lynch et al. (2024) supplies recent national evidence on summer enrichment stratification; NASEM (2019, 2025) supplies the consensus-report backdrop. The resulting 'bifurcation' claim — affluent students buy enrichment, public systems supply remediation — is a real analytic contribution to the framing and is not merely asserted.

The EL-specific strand is thin because the literature is thin, and the paper is honest about that. Arbreton et al. (2008) is flagged as lacking a comparison group. Farbman (2015), Matthews and Mellom (2012), Schneider (2020), and Lopez, Lee, and Tung (2020) are correctly described as small-scale, program-specific, or qualitative. Johnson (2020) is identified as an evaluation of one summer credit-recovery program for newcomers. Figlio and Ozek (2020) and Quintero (2024) on retention-as-extra-time are paired with the NEPC (2019) critique. The mixed-evidence characterization of EL representation in extra-time opportunities (Simpkins et al., 2011, and Yu et al., 2015, versus Camacho and Fuligni, 2015, and Lopez et al., 2020) is fair and does not stack the deck.

The interdisciplinary reach is real. Developmental psychology, sociology of education, economics of education, and qualitative EL scholarship all appear, and community-based and heritage-language education (Baldridge et al., 2017; Zhou and Li, 2003) is acknowledged rather than excluded by definition. For a quantitative AERJ paper this is broader than typical.

WHERE THE MAP IS INCOMPLETE

Economics of instructional time. This is the most consequential gap given the paper's design. The identification strategy — within-student variation in credit load, with student, school, and grade-by-year fixed effects — is the same logic used in a well-developed economics literature that the review does not reach. Cattaneo, Oggenfuss, and Wolter (2017) is cited as the methodological model, and Rivkin and Schiman (2015) appears, but I am reasonably confident that Lavy's Economic Journal work exploiting within-student across-subject variation in instructional hours across countries exists and is the canonical version of this design; that Taylor's Journal of Public Economics regression-discontinuity study of doubled middle-school math periods exists; and that Figlio, Holden, and Ozek evaluated Florida's mandated extra hour of literacy instruction using a regression discontinuity in a heavily EL-serving state.
