The last is the closest large-scale analogue to this paper's 'longer school day' finding, which accounts for 86 percent of the extra-time cases here. There is also a snow-day / instructional-days literature (Marcotte and colleagues; Goodman) and the Chilean full-school-day evidence (Bellei) that would qualify the affirmative framing. Their absence is why the sentence 'Research consistently has shown that increasing instructional time improves academic outcomes' reads as stronger than warranted: the fuller evidence base is that time effects are highly context-dependent, that some large extended-day evaluations return nulls, and that the marginal hour is worth much less than the average hour.

Double-dose. The three Chicago citations present the favorable findings. I am reasonably confident that Nomi and Allensworth published a follow-up (AERJ, roughly 2013, titled along the lines of 'Sorting and supporting') documenting that double-dose algebra raised test scores while increasing course failure rates and reorganizing classrooms by ability. Both of those side effects are directly relevant here. This paper cannot observe whether enrolled credits were earned — it says so plainly in the limitations — so a Chicago-style pattern of enrollment up, completion down would be invisible in its data. A reader who takes the course-taking results at face value without knowing about that antecedent will overestimate what 'more credits enrolled' implies.

Credit accumulation and on-track research. The paper's two most persuasive findings are that extra time roughly doubles the odds of a full academic course load in middle school and raises the odds of a regular diploma. The literature that establishes why credit accumulation predicts graduation — Allensworth and Easton's on-track indicator work, and the early-warning-indicator literature that followed — is absent. This is not a nitpick: without that framework, the full-course-load result is close to mechanical (enroll in more credits, become more likely to be enrolled in a full load), and the on-track literature is what would make it substantively interpretable. Royster et al. (2015) and Furstenberg and Neumark (2007) appear only in the Discussion as suggestions for future postsecondary work.

Credit recovery and graduation-rate inflation. This is the most important interpretive omission. The paper reports large graduation effects and essentially zero achievement effects, and interprets the divergence through instructional quality (Kraft and Novicoff's learning-time distinction) and test-validity concerns for EL students (Abedi, 2002; Witmer and Marinho, 2025). Both are reasonable. But the reading that the credit-recovery literature would supply — that credit and diploma outcomes can move substantially through credential-accumulation mechanisms without corresponding learning gains — is never entertained, even though the paper cites the descriptive credit-recovery work (U.S. Department of Education, 2018; Kuhfeld et al., 2025) and the quality-concerns work (Darling-Aduana, 2021; Darling-Aduana et al., 2024). I am reasonably confident that Heppen and colleagues' randomized trial comparing online and face-to-face algebra credit recovery exists, along with subsequent policy analysis of credit recovery's contribution to rising graduation rates. Readers should hold this alternative explanation in mind, particularly because the paper's own design cannot distinguish retaking a failed course from supplementing a passed one.

EL classification, tracking, and reclassification. Callahan (2005) and Umansky et al. (2024) anchor the tracking argument, but the broader body is under-represented. Umansky's own AERJ article on leveled and exclusionary tracking (circa 2016) is not cited, which is surprising given how squarely it supports the framing. Callahan, Wilkinson, and Muller's work on ESL placement and course-taking is absent. More importantly, the causal reclassification literature — a body of regression-discontinuity studies exploiting proficiency-test cutoffs, associated with Robinson-Cimpian and Thompson, Carlson and Knowles, Johnson, Pope, and Umansky among others — never appears, even though the paper explicitly grapples with reclassification as a post-treatment variable, reports that 55 percent of its graduation sample reclassified, and reports a supplementary finding that extra core-content time may increase reclassification. That supplementary claim is presented with an appropriate reverse-causality caveat, but it sits in a literature the paper does not acknowledge.

Synthesis anchors for summer school and tutoring. Callen et al. (2025), Lynch et al. (2024), Lauer et al. (2006), and Bennett et al. (2024) carry these strands. Cooper and colleagues' summer-school meta-analysis, Kim and Quinn's summer-reading meta-analysis, and Nickow, Oreopoulos, and Quan's tutoring meta-analysis are the standard reference points and are absent. Practically, the stakes are limited — summer accounts for 5 percent of extra-time cases and online for 1.4 percent — but the omissions contribute to the impression of a more uniformly positive time literature than exists.

NOVELTY CLAIMS ASSESSED

Claim 1: a novel statewide measure of extra instructional time that is agnostic to format, timing, and content. This holds up as a methodological contribution, with an important qualification readers should carry. The specific operationalization — total enrolled credits minus the mean credits of non-EL peers in the same school, grade, and year, with a 0.5-credit threshold — does appear to be new, and it is a clever way to sidestep the program-evaluation frame. But it is a relative credit-load measure, not a measure of instructional time. Two students with identical hours in school will differ on this measure if their peers differ. The authors concede this candidly and at some length in the Discussion ('we suspect that many students that we identified as receiving extra instruction simply had fuller high school schedules'), which is to their credit, but the abstract, title, and conclusion all use the stronger 'extra instructional time' language. Antecedents: transcript-based course-taking analysis is a mature tradition (NCES high school transcript studies, Callahan's work, the authors' own 2024 multistate paper); the novelty is the peer-referenced differential, not statewide transcript analysis.

Claim 2: causal estimates of extra time for secondary EL students. This is defensible but narrower than it sounds. Johnson (2020), published in this same journal and cited here, already supplies a quasi-experimental secondary-level estimate of one form of extra time (summer credit recovery) on credit accumulation for newcomer EL students, with a positive result. Figlio and Ozek (2020) supplies a strong regression-discontinuity estimate for EL students, though for early-grade retention. So the genuinely new element is coverage — all EL subgroups, all formats, statewide, with achievement and diploma-type outcomes — rather than the existence of causal estimates. The paper also repeatedly and appropriately downgrades its own causal language ('our best estimates of the causal effects rather than definitive causal estimates'; graduation results 'exploratory' and 'tentative'), so the claim is not oversold in the analysis sections even where the framing is looser.

Claim 3 (implicit): that prior work has focused predominantly on small-scale interventions. This undersells the economics literature, which includes statewide and cross-national designs. Readers should not take this framing as an accurate description of the field.

ENGAGEMENT WITH CONFLICTING EVIDENCE

Mixed. The literature review leans affirmative; the Discussion is considerably more self-critical than the review. Genuine engagement with the null achievement result appears in the Discussion, including three plausible competing explanations (extra time went to electives; instructional quality was low; standardized tests in English mismeasure EL content knowledge). The paper also acknowledges the possibility of negative effects from low-quality extra time (disengagement, weaker student-teacher relationships, citing Darling-Aduana et al., 2024). What is missing is engagement with the two literatures whose findings most directly threaten the paper's headline: the double-dose course-failure finding and the credit-recovery credential-inflation finding. A reader working from this paper alone would not know either exists.

CITATION ACCURACY

I cross-checked every in-text citation against the reference list. Two real defects:

1. Mulhern (2023) is cited in the Methods to motivate the school-counselor FTE covariate and has no reference-list entry. The intended source is almost certainly Mulhern's American Economic Review article on individual school counselors' effects on educational attainment, but readers cannot confirm this from the paper.

2. 'Kim, 2024' in the shadow-education paragraph maps to a reference-list entry by Kim, Goodman, and West (2024) on private tutoring centers, and should read 'Kim et al., 2024.' Anyone chasing that claim will search for the wrong article.

Smaller irregularities worth noticing: stray commas in 'Buchmann, et al, 2010' and 'Snellman, et al., 2015'; the Figlio and Ozek (2020) entry gives article number 104155 but a DOI ending 104184 (one is wrong); Quintero (2024) is formatted as a November 2024 conference presentation but linked to an Annenberg working-paper file numbered ai25-1247, suggesting a 2025 working paper; and the reference list is misalphabetized in at least three places (AASA before Abedi, Kim before Kieffer, Jimenez-Castellanos after Johnson). Several key sources are gray literature or unpublished at time of writing — Kraft and Novicoff (2024) as an EdWorkingPaper, Darling-Aduana et al. (2024) as an EdWorkingPaper, Quintero (2024), Shin et al. (2026) as a conference presentation — so readers should check whether peer-reviewed versions now exist and whether the findings changed.

I did not find substantive mischaracterization of any cited study's findings. Descriptions are generally cautious and the caveats attached to weak studies are accurate. The problems are of omission and of framing emphasis, not of misrepresentation.

SELF-CITATION AND INDEPENDENCE

The research team cites its own work heavily: Umansky et al. (2024) appears at least six times and supplies the paper's central theoretical construct (ELD crowd out); Thompson et al. (2026), Bromley et al. (2025), Shin et al. (2026), and Vazquez Cano et al. (2021) also appear. Given that this team is the leading source on secondary EL course access and that the work was conducted under the IES-funded National Research and Development Center for Secondary English Learners, the self-citation is substantively warranted. But readers should be aware that the theoretical frame has not been independently replicated, and that the empirical corroboration offered here is by the same team using data from a state included in the earlier multistate study. That is not a flaw; it is a fact about the evidentiary independence of the finding.

BOTTOM LINE FOR READERS

This is a well-organized, honest, and interdisciplinary review that accurately maps a genuinely thin EL-specific literature and somewhat over-flatters a mixed general literature. Cite it for the statewide descriptive picture of relative credit load among secondary EL students in Oregon, which is new and well-documented, and for the observation that 'fuller schedules' may be a largely invisible lever schools use to allocate time differentially — an argument the authors make in the Discussion that is arguably more original than the causal estimates. Do not cite it as a complete account of the instructional-time evidence base, and do not read its graduation finding without holding the credit-recovery literature's credentialing-versus-learning question in mind.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper is unusually well organized — a single set of research-question headings is carried in parallel through the literature review, method, and findings, which makes it easy to navigate and easy to read selectively. But the exposition does not survive close checking against the exhibits: the sample size in the Data section does not match Table 1, one odds ratio is mistyped by a factor of ten, one is converted to the wrong percentage, one ELA coefficient quoted in the text appears in no column of Table 7, a Table 8 panel is mislabeled, and the significance-star convention changes meaning from table to table with two tables carrying no legend at all. The abstract and conclusion are also noticeably stronger than the Findings section they summarize, dropping the paper's own "exploratory" framing of the graduation results and its central caveat that most "extra time" is probably a fuller schedule rather than a program.

**Strengths:**

- Exceptionally clear architecture. The three RQ1 sub-questions (who gets extra time, how do they receive it, what is it used for) are used verbatim as headings in the literature review, the analytic method, and the findings. A reader can read all three passes on a single sub-question by jumping between three points in the paper, which is rare and genuinely useful.
- The measurement section (pp. 12–14) is a model of transparency about a novel construct. The four variants of the treatment (binary/continuous × any/core), the 0.5-credit threshold and its rationale, the same-school/grade/year non-EL comparison, and the credit-coding rules are all stated plainly and in one place.
- The Findings section itself is mostly disciplined. It repeatedly reminds the reader that the estimates are relative to non-EL peers (p. 19), it labels the graduation results "exploratory" at the point of presentation (p. 29), and it applies Kraft's (2020) benchmark to call the 0.022 SD ELA effect "very small and not reaching a policy-relevant magnitude" (p. 27) rather than leaning on statistical significance.
- The Discussion is intellectually honest in one important respect that most papers duck: the section "Supplemental Supports? Fuller Schedules? Repeated Coursework?" (pp. 33–34) explicitly concedes that what the authors measured as "extra instructional time" may largely be fuller schedules rather than designed supplemental instruction, and even reports that state leaders pushed back on the interpretation.
- Table 4 and Table 5 carry full, self-contained notes that define every operationalization (what counts as a summer course, an online course, concurrent enrollment, a longer day), so those two exhibits can be read without the method section.
- Footnote 1 (terminology) and footnote 3 (why "electives" is broader than it sounds, because Oregon requires several of them for graduation) are placed exactly where a skeptical reader would raise the objection.

**Weaknesses:**

- Sample size in the text does not match the tables. The Data section (p. 9) reports "32,673 students (64,162 observations)"; Table 1 (p. 11) and Table 2 (p. 20) both report 64,241 student-year observations and 32,685 students. Nothing in the paper reconciles the two.
- A mistyped estimate in the graduation results. On p. 32 the text reports "OR = 0.0464" for the 4-year modified-diploma effect; Table 8 (p. 30) shows 0.464. The accompanying "54% lower" is correct for 0.464, so the printed OR has an extra zero.
- An arithmetic error in the same paragraph. The text (p. 32) says the odds of a modified diploma were "88% lower after 5 years (OR = 0.175)." An odds ratio of 0.175 is 82.5% lower, not 88%; 88% would require an OR near 0.12. Neither 0.175 nor the unmatched 0.188 in Table 8 yields 88%.
- A quoted coefficient that is in no column of the table. The text (p. 27) reports the "any" credit differential's effect on ELA as "0.010 SD units." Table 7 (p. 29) shows 0.028 (Model 1), 0.011 (Model 2), and 0.012 (Model 3, the preferred model). The prose figure matches none of them.
- Table 8's continued panel (p. 31) is headed "Four-year outcomes" but contains the five-year core-content results — the four-year core rows already appear on p. 30, and the text cites this panel's 0.175 as a five-year estimate. Readers landing on p. 31 will read five-year results as four-year results.
- Significance stars mean different things in different tables and are undefined in two of them. Table 5 (p. 26): * = p<.05. Table 6 (p. 28): * = p<.001. Table 7 (p. 29): * = p<.1. Table 3 (pp. 22–23) and Table 8 (pp. 30–31) have no note and no legend at all, and Table 8 uses up to four asterisks, which appear nowhere else. The p-values the text attaches to Table 8 imply yet a fourth convention (* = p<.1, ** = p<.05, *** = p<.01, **** = p<.001). No star in this paper can be read without checking which table it is in.
- Table 3 has no note whatsoever — no significance legend, no clustering statement, and no explanation of why its N is 53,311 when Tables 1 and 2 report 64,241. Roughly 11,000 observations (17%) drop out of the paper's main descriptive models with no comment anywhere in the text.
- Table 1's graduation rows invite a serious misreading. They show a 4-year graduation rate of 0.20 and a 5-year rate of 0.15 — a five-year rate cannot be lower than a four-year rate if both are cumulative — and the 5-year regular-diploma rate (0.16) exceeds the 5-year graduation rate (0.15), which is impossible since regular diplomas are a subset of graduations. The note does not say that the denominator is all grade 6–12 student-years, so a reader can easily mistake 0.20 for an EL graduation rate, against the 68% figure the paper itself cites on p. 8.
- Two subgroup panels in Table 2 (pp. 20–21) do not reconcile to the reported total. The reading-achievement rows sum to 63,539 rather than 64,241 because the "Missing" N (35,986) is identical to the math "Missing" N, even though Table 1 gives different missingness rates (0.56 math vs. 0.57 reading). The home-language rows sum to 63,587, short by 654.
- The home-language categories in the tables do not match the ones the method section names. The Method (p. 13) and Study Context (p. 8) both say the five most common languages are Spanish, Vietnamese, Arabic, Russian, and Chinese; Tables 1, 2, and 3 report Chinese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Russian, and English — Arabic never appears in any exhibit. Table 1's note compounds this by calling these "the top five non-English languages" when one of the five listed categories is English.
- A Discussion claim is contradicted by the paper's own descriptive table. Page 33 states that "extra instructional time was roughly equally allocated to core and non-core academic courses." Table 5's Total row (p. 26) shows the with/without-extra-time gap as 0.23 credits across all four core subjects versus 0.61 in electives plus 0.11 in ELD — roughly a 1:3 split, not an even one. The Findings section says the opposite of the Discussion: "when EL-classified students received extra time, that time typically went to increased enrollment in electives and ELD" (p. 25).
- The Discussion (p. 33) and Conclusion (p. 37) both state that "newcomer students, long-term ELs, and ELs with disabilities" are more likely to receive extra time, without saying that this holds only in one of the two treatment definitions and reverses in the other. In Table 3, long-term ELs are not significantly different in the "any" model (OR = 0.958, n.s.) and are only elevated in core (1.244); dually identified students are elevated in "any" (1.241) but significantly *less* likely in core (0.751) and take 0.183 fewer core credits. The Findings section reports the reversal correctly (p. 21); the Discussion and Conclusion drop it.
- The abstract escalates beyond the results. It states that extra time "substantially increased the likelihood of their enrolling in a full course load and graduating with a regular diploma." The graduation result is labeled "exploratory" in the Findings (p. 29) and "tentative" in the Method (p. 18); the strongest 4-year regular-diploma estimate is significant only at p<.1 (OR = 1.464); the "any" 4-year estimate is null (1.133); and Appendix Table A7 shows no significant effect at all when diploma type is ignored. The abstract mentions none of this.
- The abstract also omits the paper's two most important interpretive caveats: that EL-classified students as a group receive *less* instructional time than peers (−0.21 core credits, −0.02 total), and that most of what is measured as extra time is probably a fuller schedule rather than a supplemental program — the point the Discussion spends three pages on. A reader who stops at the abstract will take away a program-evaluation finding the paper does not claim to have.
- Unit slippage between students and student-years. The abstract, findings, and discussion all speak of "one in five EL-classified students," but the 18% figure in Table 2 is a share of 64,241 student-years. Table 1 separately reports 5,450 students with extra time out of 32,685, and the note never explains how a student who had extra time in one of three observed years is assigned to a column.
- A definitional drift in the RQ1c results. The Method (p. 14) defines core-content displacement as a student "lacking one or more of the four core content area classes"; the Findings (p. 25) gloss the same 32% figure as students who "never enrolled in an ELA, math, science, or social studies course that year," which describes lacking all four. These are very different populations.
- The Findings describe Model 3 as including "student, grade, and school by year fixed effects" (p. 25), which contradicts both Equation 3 (p. 16) and Table 6's own note — both of which specify grade-by-year and school fixed effects.
- Smaller production lapses that a reader will notice: Table 1 prints "0.o6" (letter o) for the core time differential; Table 3 is labeled "Odd ratios"; Table 6's note reads "Standard are errors in parentheses"; the text has "mutliracial" (p. 21), "Els" (p. 8), and "2 of more years" (p. 32); Table 1 and Table 2 notes both give the assessment window as "2015–16 to 2016–19"; Mulhern (2023) is cited on p. 14 but is absent from the reference list; Kim et al. (2024) is cited as "Kim, 2024" (p. 3); and the reference list misorders Johnson before Jimenez-Castellanos and Kim before Kieffer.
- A large share of load-bearing evidence is online-only. The supplemental/displacement tabulations behind the 55% and 32% figures (Appendix A6), the matched-sample balance checks (A2), the reclassification analysis (A3), the inverse-probability-weighting results (A5), and the combined-diploma null results (A7) are all in the online supplement. The last of these matters most: the finding that the regular- and modified-diploma effects "cancel each other out" is reported in one sentence on p. 32 with the evidence itself off-page.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the Findings section (pp. 19–32) as the authoritative account and treat the Discussion and Conclusion as a looser summary. Where they disagree — on how extra time is allocated between core and electives, and on which subgroups receive it — the Findings text is the one that matches the tables.
- Do not quote any number from the graduation paragraph on p. 32 without opening Table 8. Three of the four figures in it have a problem: the OR printed as 0.0464 is 0.464 in the table; the "88% lower" should be 82.5% for the OR of 0.175 that is cited alongside it; and the panel that OR comes from is headed "Four-year outcomes" on p. 31 when it is in fact the five-year core result.
- Before citing any starred estimate, find that specific table's legend — a single asterisk means p<.05 in Table 5, p<.001 in Table 6, and p<.1 in Table 7, and Tables 3 and 8 have no legend at all. For Table 8 in particular, the only guide to what its one-to-four asterisks mean is the p-values the text attaches to four of its cells on p. 32, which imply * = p<.1 through **** = p<.001.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns.*

- If you want the paper's headline achievement number, take 0.022 SD (ELA, core credit differential, Model 3) from Table 7 directly. The companion figure for the "any" differential is given as 0.010 in the text but is 0.012 in Model 3 of the table.
- Read Table 1's four graduation rows with the denominator in mind: they are shares of all grade 6–12 student-years, not graduation cohorts, which is why the 4-year rate reads as 0.20 against the 68% state EL graduation rate cited on p. 8. The 5-year rows in particular (0.15 graduation, 0.16 regular diploma) cannot be read as cumulative rates.
- Tables 2 and 3 are the core of RQ1 and repay slow reading, but check the columns you rely on: the reading-achievement and home-language subgroup Ns do not sum to the 64,241 total, and Table 3 is estimated on 53,311 observations with no explanation given anywhere.
- When reading Table 2's last two rows, note that the "any" and "core" treatment groups largely do not overlap — only 29% of students with any extra time also have core extra time, and only 32% of those with core extra time have any extra time. The paper never flags this, but it is essential for interpreting why the "any" and "core" results diverge so sharply throughout.
- Treat Table 4's 86% "longer school day" figure as a definition, not an observation. The note makes clear it is the residual category — assigned when no summer, online, or concurrent enrollment is detected — so it is not evidence that schools ran extended-day programs. The Discussion (pp. 33–34) says as much and is the more careful statement.
- The literature review (pp. 3–7) is thorough and well organized but is safely skimmable for a reader who knows the instructional-time literature; the Study Context section (pp. 8–9) should not be skipped, because Oregon's modified-diploma option is what makes the graduation findings interpretable.
- Do not read the abstract alone. It presents the graduation effect as established when the paper labels it exploratory and tentative, and it omits both that EL-classified students on average receive less instructional time than peers and that most measured "extra time" is likely a fuller schedule rather than a designed program.
- If you intend to cite the 55% supplemental / 32% displacement figures from p. 25, note that the underlying tabulation is online-only (Appendix Table A6) and that the in-text gloss of displacement ("never enrolled in an ELA, math, science, or social studies course") does not match the definition given in the Method ("lacking one or more of the four core content area classes").
- The single most important omission for a reader weighing the graduation claim is Appendix Table A7, summarized in one sentence on p. 32: with diploma type ignored, there is no significant graduation effect. Anyone citing this paper for "extra time increases graduation" should retrieve that appendix table first.

**Detailed Commentary:**

ORGANIZATION AND NAVIGABILITY

The paper's structure is its strongest feature. Two research questions are posed on p. 3, RQ1 with three sub-questions. Those three sub-questions then become headings, in the same order and nearly the same words, in three separate places: the literature review (pp. 3–7, twice — once for the general population and once for EL-classified students), the analytic method (pp. 14–16), and the findings (pp. 19–25). This lets a reader who cares only about, say, instructional formats read three short passages instead of the whole paper. Very few empirical papers are this navigable.

The cost is that the load-bearing evidence is spread across eight in-text tables and at least seven online appendix tables plus an Appendix B. Several of the appendix items are not optional: A6 holds the supplemental/displacement tabulation that the Discussion builds a section on; A7 holds the combined-diploma null result that materially qualifies the paper's most-quoted claim; A2 holds the matched-sample balance evidence on which the graduation causal claim rests; A5 holds the IPW results that the authors mention and then decline to discuss. A reader without journal access to the supplement cannot evaluate the graduation findings.

INTERNAL CONSISTENCY — SPECIFIC DISAGREEMENTS

Sample sizes. Data section, p. 9: "totaling 32,673 students (64,162 observations)." Table 1, p. 11: 64,241 student-year observations, 32,685 students. Table 2, p. 20, total row: 64,241. The Table 1 column Ns are internally coherent (11,881 + 52,360 = 64,241; 5,450 + 27,235 = 32,685), so the text's pair of figures is the outlier. Table 3 (pp. 22–23) then reports 53,311 observations in all four columns — an unexplained 17% loss, presumably listwise deletion on prior-achievement covariates, but the paper never says so and Table 3 has no note.

Table 2 subgroup panels. Six of the eight panels sum exactly to 64,241 (EL subgroup, FRPL, race/ethnicity, grade, math achievement, ELP level). Two do not. Reading achievement sums to 63,539: its "Missing" cell reads 35,986, byte-for-byte the math "Missing" cell, even though Table 1 reports math missing at 0.56 and reading missing at 0.57 — the reading figure should be roughly 36,688. Home language sums to 63,587, short by 654.

Home-language categories. Method, p. 13: "the five most commonly spoken languages—Spanish, Vietnamese, Arabic, Russian, and Chinese." Study Context, p. 8: "Spanish, Russian, Vietnamese, Chinese, and Arabic." Tables 1, 2, and 3: Chinese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Russian, English. Arabic appears in no exhibit; English appears in every exhibit and is never named in the text as a category. Table 1's note describes these as "the top five non-English languages," which is not what the table shows.

Table 1 graduation rows. As printed: graduation rate (4 year) 0.20, regular diploma (4 year) 0.16, graduation rate (5 year) 0.15, regular diploma (5 year) 0.16. Two impossibilities on the face of it — a 5-year cumulative rate below the 4-year rate, and a diploma subtype exceeding the total graduation rate it belongs to. The note explains the assessments used but says nothing about the graduation denominators, and the primary sample spans grades 6–12, so most student-years are not graduation-eligible. Against the 68% four-year EL graduation rate the paper itself cites on p. 8, an unwary reader will misread 0.20 badly.

Table 3 quotations in text. These check out. p. 19: newcomer 23% higher odds (table: 1.231); dually identified 24% higher (1.241); economically disadvantaged +0.13 credits (0.126); grades 11 and 12 at 0.18 and 0.38 credits (0.184, 0.384); intercept −0.28 (−0.280). p. 21: newcomer core 13% (1.133); long-term core 24% (1.244); dually identified core 25% lower (0.751); Asian/Pacific Islander core 31% higher (1.314); Chinese 0.557 and Vietnamese 0.587; ELP 18% higher odds (1.177); core intercept −0.29 (−0.294). The arithmetic claim that "only in 12th grade did positive differences fully offset this negative baseline" also checks (−0.280 + 0.384 = +0.104; grade 11 gives −0.096).

One framing problem in that passage: the text says EL students "overall enrolled in significantly less total instructional time than their non-EL peers, reflected in the −0.28 intercept." The intercept is the fitted value for the reference profile (developmental EL, not economically disadvantaged, White, Spanish-speaking, 9th grade, mean achievement), not the population average, which Table 2 reports as −0.02. Both facts are true; the sentence attributes the wrong one to the wrong quantity.

Table 4 quotations. All check: longer day 86% (0.859), summer 5% (0.050), online 1.4% (0.014), multiple formats ~7% (0.074); core versions 65% (0.653), 2% (0.024), 1% (0.010), 4% (0.039). Note that the table's own definition makes "longer school day" a residual — it is assigned when none of the other formats is observed — so the 86% is definitional rather than an observation about school programs. The Discussion is candid about this; the Findings sentence "longer school days served as the primary mechanism for delivering extra time" (p. 25) reads more strongly than the construction supports.

Table 5 and the allocation claim. Table 5's Total row differences: ELA 0.07, math 0.03, science 0.02, social studies 0.11, ELD 0.11, electives 0.61. Core total = 0.23; non-core total = 0.72; the sum, 0.95, matches Table 2's 7.58 − 6.61 = 0.97 to rounding. Every one of these Total-row values also reconciles exactly with Table 1's corresponding with/without columns, which is good. Against this, the Discussion sentence on p. 33 — "Extra instructional time was roughly equally allocated to core and non-core academic courses" — is wrong by roughly a factor of three, and contradicts the Findings' own statement on p. 25 that extra time "typically went to increased enrollment in electives and ELD." (The claim is closer to defensible against Table 6's fixed-effects estimates — middle school 0.367 core vs. 0.516 elective+ELD — but the Discussion does not say it is drawing on Table 6, and the descriptive exhibit says otherwise.) A minor related overreach: p. 25 says students with extra time "enrolled in slightly more credits across core content areas," but Table 5's grade-6 ELA difference is −0.04*, i.e. significantly fewer.

Table 6 quotations. All check. Middle school Model 3 core credits sum to 0.367 exactly (0.108 + 0.104 + 0.054 + 0.101), the range 0.054–0.108 is right, electives 0.397 is right, and the full-load OR of 1.996 is right. High school Model 3 core sums to 0.430, matching "0.43 credit in total." The high-school full-load OR of 1.597 is correctly described as "a 60% increase in the odds." One loose usage: the middle-school result is described as having "doubled a given student's likelihood" of full-load enrollment; an OR of 2.0 doubles the odds, not the probability, and the paper states the odds interpretation correctly one sentence later for high school. Table 6's note deserves credit for explaining, unprompted, why the full-load Ns (4,857 and 5,007) are so much smaller than the credit-enrollment Ns (26,461 and 12,104) — fixed-effects logit drops non-switchers. Also worth a reader's notice: the BIC values favor Model 2 over the "preferred" Model 3 in both school levels, and the paper does not comment.

Table 7 quotations. The core-differential ELA result, 0.022 SD at p<.01, matches Model 3. The companion "any" figure quoted as "0.010 SD units" matches no column: Model 1 is 0.028, Model 2 is 0.011, Model 3 is 0.012. The characterization (small, nonsignificant) is unaffected, but the printed number is wrong.

Table 8 quotations. Four numbers are quoted on p. 32 and three have problems. (a) "OR = 0.0464" for the 4-year core modified-diploma effect — Table 8 shows 0.464; the accompanying "54% lower" confirms 0.464 is intended. (b) "88% lower after 5 years (OR = 0.175)" — 0.175 implies 82.5% lower; 88% would need an OR near 0.12; the unmatched estimate in the same row, 0.188, gives 81%. (c) That 0.175 sits in the continued panel on p. 31, which is headed "Four-year outcomes" but must be the five-year core block, since the four-year core rows already appear on p. 30 and the text cites it as five-year. (d) "OR = 1.464, p<.1" and "OR = 1.792, p<.05" match the table's values; their stars (* and **) do not match the conventions used in Tables 5, 6, or 7.

Table 8 also labels its counts "No. of student-year observations," but the graduation dataset is explicitly described on p. 9 as condensing each student's high school career into a single observation. And the Ns cannot be reconstructed: p. 9 gives a graduation sample of N = 2,130; p. 18 says CEM retained 77% for the any models and 72% for the core models, implying about 1,640 and 1,534; Table 8 reports 1,383 and 1,338 for the four-year regular-diploma models and different figures again (1,259 and 1,136) for the modified-diploma models, with no explanation of why the same matched sample changes size by outcome. The five-year Ns (882, 845, 767, 730) are smaller still, presumably because fewer cohorts have five-year outcomes, but this is never stated. Finally, the columns "Matching 1," "Matching 2," and "Matching 3" are distinguished only by X marks on three control rows, with no note explaining the sequence and no statement of which is preferred — though the text quotes Matching 3 throughout. This matters, because Matching 1 estimates are uniformly closer to 1 and nonsignificant for the regular-diploma outcomes (1.029, 1.244, 1.111, 1.285), so which column a reader treats as the result changes the paper's conclusion.

SIGNIFICANCE-STAR CONVENTIONS

This is the single most consequential consistency problem, because it silently corrupts any star a reader reads. Table 5's note: * p<.05, ** p<.01, *** p<.001. Table 6's note: * p<.001 (single convention). Table 7's note: * p<.1, ** p<.01, *** p<.001. Tables 3 and 8 have no note and no legend, and Table 8 uses four asterisks, a level that appears nowhere else in the paper. The p-values the text attaches to Table 8's cells on p. 32 imply a fifth scheme (* p<.1, ** p<.05, *** p<.01, **** p<.001). So a single asterisk in this paper means p<.05, p<.001, or p<.1 depending on the page; "***" means p<.001 in Tables 5 and 7 but p<.01 per the text's reading of Table 8.

ABSTRACT FIDELITY

The abstract is accurate on two of its three claims and overstated on the third. "Roughly one in five EL-classified students received extra time" is right (18% of student-years, though the abstract says "students"). "Extra instruction had only minimal effects on standardized test achievement" is right and appropriately deflationary. But "substantially increased the likelihood of their enrolling in a full course load and graduating with a regular diploma" merges a well-identified fixed-effects result with a matching result the paper elsewhere calls "exploratory" (p. 29) and "tentative" (p. 18), whose strongest four-year regular-diploma estimate is significant only at p<.1, whose "any"-treatment four-year estimate is null, and which the paper reports washes out entirely when diploma type is not distinguished (Appendix A7).

Two omissions matter as much as the overstatement. First, the abstract never says that EL-classified students on average receive less instructional time than their non-EL peers (−0.21 core credits, −0.02 total) — arguably the paper's most striking descriptive finding and the one that frames its equity argument. Second, the abstract never signals that "extra instructional time" here means a credit differential relative to same-school non-EL peers rather than participation in any identified program, nor that the Discussion concludes most of it is probably just a fuller schedule. A reader who stops at the abstract will come away believing an intervention was evaluated.

The Conclusion (p. 37) repeats the escalation: "We found positive effects of this exposure on enrollment in a full courseload and, importantly, on graduating with a regular diploma," with no hedge, and it repeats the Discussion's conflated subgroup claim about newcomers, long-term ELs, and ELs with disabilities that Table 3 supports only if one silently switches between the any and core specifications.

SMALLER ITEMS A READER WILL HIT

Method/Findings mismatch on fixed effects: Equation 3 (p. 16) and Table 6's note specify grade-by-year and school fixed effects; the Findings (p. 25) describe Model 3 as "student, grade, and school by year fixed effects." Definitional drift on displacement: Method p. 14, "lacking one or more of the four core content area classes"; Findings p. 25, "never enrolled in an ELA, math, science, or social studies course that year." Table 1 prints "0.o6" for the core time differential (Table 2 and the text both give 0.06). Table 3's column label reads "Odd ratios." Table 6's note reads "Standard are errors in parentheses." Table 1 and Table 2 notes both date ELPA21 to "2015–16 to 2016–19." Typos: "mutliracial" (p. 21), "88% of former Els" (p. 8), "2 of more years" (p. 32). Citation problems: Mulhern (2023) is cited on p. 14 and is absent from the reference list; Kim et al. (2024) is cited as "Kim, 2024" on p. 3; the reference list places Johnson before Jimenez-Castellanos and Kim before Kieffer. Table 1's note refers to "all other 234 languages" while listing five categories, one of which is English. Finally, the Study Context (pp. 8–9) draws all its descriptive statistics from a 2023–25 ODE report for a study covering 2013–14 through 2018–19, without noting the mismatch.

WHAT TO SKIM, WHAT NOT TO SKIP

Skimmable: the literature review (pp. 3–7) for anyone familiar with the instructional-time or EL course-access literatures; the "Comparing Extra Instructional Time With Other Interventions" section (p. 36), which is speculative; the Limitations section, which is honest but contains no surprises.

Do not skip: the Key Variables section (pp. 12–14), because nothing in the paper is interpretable without knowing what the credit differential is and is not; Table 2 and Table 3 for RQ1; the "Supplemental Supports? Fuller Schedules? Repeated Coursework?" section (pp. 33–34), which is where the paper most honestly bounds its own claim and which the abstract omits entirely; and the single sentence on p. 32 reporting that the regular- and modified-diploma effects cancel when diploma type is ignored.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT

The prose itself is clear, the structure is better than most papers in the field, and the Findings section is written with genuine care about not overclaiming. Rated "adequate" rather than "strong" because the density of text–table disagreements — a mistyped odds ratio, a wrong percentage conversion, a coefficient in no column, a mislabeled table panel, a sample size that does not match Table 1, two subgroup panels that do not sum, five different significance conventions across five tables (two of them undefined), and a Discussion allocation claim contradicted by the paper's own Table 5 — means a reader cannot safely quote this paper's prose without opening the corresponding exhibit each time. That is a real and repeated cost, not a stylistic quibble. Rated above "weak" because comprehension is never actually blocked: the argument is followable, the exhibits are mostly well documented, and nearly all the errors are recoverable by a reader who checks.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's durable contribution is descriptive and measurement-based: a novel, program-agnostic way of detecting extra credit-bearing instructional time from statewide course records (a student's enrolled credits relative to non-EL peers in the same school, grade, and year), applied to every secondary EL-classified student in Oregon over six years. That descriptive portrait -- how rare extra time is, that it is overwhelmingly delivered as a fuller in-school schedule rather than summer or online programming, that most of it flows to electives and ELD rather than core content, and that a third of recipients still lack a full academic load -- is genuinely new and is the part of the paper the field should absorb. The causal half is much weaker than the abstract implies: the course-taking 'effects' are close to accounting identities, the achievement null is the best-identified estimate in the paper, and the graduation result is a small, borderline-significant, Oregon-specific diploma-type substitution that disappears when diploma types are combined.

**Strengths:**

- Genuine measurement innovation with reusable value: prior work could only study extra time where a named program existed (a summer school, a double-dose class, an after-school site). Defining extra time as a within-school-grade-year credit differential against non-EL peers makes extra time visible at scale from ordinary state course records, is agnostic to format and provider, and is portable to any state with course-level SCED data. The authors' own framing of this -- that the literature 'may be overlooking a primary means that schools have at their disposal to differentially allocate instructional time (i.e., providing fuller schedules)' -- is the paper's sharpest and most transferable idea.
- Fills a real, specific gap. The prior EL-specific literature on extra time is a handful of single-program, single-district, or qualitative studies (Farbman 2015; Matthews and Mellom 2012; Johnson 2020; Lopez et al. 2020), plus retention studies (Figlio and Ozek 2020; Quintero 2024) whose 'extra time' is grade repetition. Nobody had a statewide, population-level answer to who among EL-classified students gets extra credit-bearing time, in what format, and toward what subjects. This paper now supplies that for one state.
- The negative-baseline framing is an important and underappreciated result. The headline number that gets quoted (18 percent receive extra time) sits on top of a population mean credit differential of -0.02 (any) and -0.21 (core), and a regression intercept of -0.28 (any) / -0.29 (core). The paper is careful to say that no subgroup except 12th graders closes the total-credit gap and that no subgroup at all closes the core-content gap. This reframes 'extra time for ELs' as a small carve-out inside a systematic deficit -- a more useful takeaway for policy than the prevalence figure.
- The allocation finding is the most policy-relevant thing in the paper and is well supported by simple, transparent evidence. Table 5 shows that the total credit gap between EL students with and without extra time is +0.61 in electives versus +0.07 ELA, +0.03 math, +0.02 science, +0.11 social studies, +0.11 ELD -- i.e., roughly two-thirds of 'extra' time lands outside core content. Paired with the finding that 32 percent of extra-time recipients still are not in a full core load, this is a concrete, actionable equity finding that does not depend on any causal claim.
- The achievement null is precisely estimated and honestly reported. With ~27,400 student-year observations and standard errors of 0.008 SD, the paper can rule out anything above roughly 0.03 SD per additional credit; the authors explicitly invoke Kraft (2020) to call the one significant estimate (0.022 SD, ELA, core credits) below policy relevance rather than spinning it. Against a literature that reports 'small to moderate gains' from extended time, a well-powered null for a large EL population is a real contribution.
- The limitations section is unusually candid, and one passage in particular ('we suspect that many students that we identified as receiving "extra" instruction simply had fuller high school schedules') gives readers the interpretive key to the whole paper. Practitioner and state-leader member checks are used to qualify the summer/online undercount rather than to advertise rigor.
- Strong descriptive attention to diploma type. Documenting that EL-classified students are two to five times over-represented among Oregon's modified-diploma earners, and that extra time is associated with movement away from that diploma, surfaces a form of stratification that is invisible in federally reported graduation rates.

**Weaknesses:**

- The central construct does not identify the thing the title and abstract promise. 'Extra instructional time' here is a relative credit differential, not receipt of a supplemental program. The authors concede this in the discussion, but the abstract, conclusion, and title do not carry the caveat. The problem is sharpest by grade: 53 percent of 12th graders and 37 percent of 11th graders are flagged as receiving extra time (any), and the authors themselves explain why -- non-EL peers finish requirements early and reduce their loads, so the comparison mean falls. A measure that mechanically flags more EL students as 'treated' precisely because their comparison group is leaving school early is measuring schedule fullness relative to a shrinking denominator, not provision of extra instruction.
- The course-taking 'effects' (Table 6) are close to arithmetic. Regressing subject-area credits on the total credit differential decomposes where the extra credits went; summing the middle-school Model 3 coefficients (0.108 math + 0.104 ELA + 0.054 science + 0.101 social studies + 0.397 electives + 0.119 ELD) gives 0.883 of a credit per additional credit, i.e. the components nearly exhaust the total by construction. The abstract's claim that extra time 'substantially increased the likelihood of enrolling in a full course load' inherits this: taking more classes mechanically raises the chance of covering all four core areas. This is a useful allocation table; it is not evidence about an intervention.
- The graduation result -- the paper's most quotable causal claim -- is the weakest analysis in it. It rests on a 2,130-student ninth-grade sample reduced to roughly 1,338-1,383 matched observations (845-882 for five-year models), is estimated by coarsened exact matching with no design-based source of exogenous variation, and is internally inconsistent across specifications: the four-year regular-diploma estimate is 1.133 (ns) for 'any' and 1.464 at only p < .1 for 'core', while the five-year estimate is 1.792 (p < .05) for 'any' but 1.488 (ns) for 'core'. The authors themselves label these 'exploratory' and 'tentative.' The abstract calls them 'substantially increased.'
- Critically, the paper reports (via Supplementary Table A7) that once regular and modified diplomas are combined, there is no significant effect on graduating at all. The finding is therefore about diploma type -- substitution away from Oregon's modified diploma -- not about whether more students graduate. A reader who takes the abstract at face value will cite this paper for an attainment effect it does not show.
- The 'distributed progressively' claim is overstated and partly contradicted by the paper's own Table 3. Dually identified students have higher odds of any extra time (OR 1.241) but 25 percent LOWER odds of extra core-content time (OR 0.751) and a significantly negative core credit differential (-0.183); the discussion and conclusion nonetheless list 'ELs with disabilities' among the groups 'more likely to receive extra time.' Higher English proficiency predicts more core extra time (OR 1.177), and higher math achievement predicts less (OR 0.855) -- a mixed, not uniformly progressive, pattern. Descriptively (Table 2), extra-time rates are close to flat across most subgroups (roughly 0.16 to 0.24 for 'any'), with grade level, not need, the dominant gradient.
- The abstract's 'roughly one in five' and the discussion's 'fewer than one in five' describe the same 18 percent; the abstract rounds in the direction that makes the phenomenon sound more common, and it is the abstract that will be quoted.
- Two ingredients that would determine what extra time actually means are absent: the data cannot say whether enrolled credits were earned, so course retakes after failure cannot be separated from genuine supplementation (a first-order distinction for interpreting both allocation and effects); and there is no measure of instructional quality or content, which the authors acknowledge is the leading explanation for the achievement null. Summer and online enrollment are known to be undercounted, so the striking '86 percent longer school day' format finding is partly definitional -- 'longer school day' is the residual category assigned when no other format is observed.
- The most striking result is the least generalizable one. The modified/regular diploma distinction that drives the graduation finding is an Oregon policy artifact created in 2009; states without a comparable second-tier diploma have no margin on which this effect could operate. The paper does not flag this boundary. More broadly, the setting is one state, pre-COVID (2013-14 to 2018-19), where 67 percent of districts serve fewer than 5 percent EL students -- a low-density context whose scheduling constraints may differ substantially from California, Texas, or New York.
- The graduation sample is uncomfortable in a way the paper does not fully resolve: 55 percent of it reclassified during high school, the main panel drops students on reclassification, and reclassification is explicitly post-treatment (Appendix A3 suggests core extra time may itself raise reclassification odds). Students who reclassify early have mechanically fewer EL-classified years in which to accumulate the '2 or more years of extra time' treatment, and reclassification strongly predicts graduation. The direction of the resulting bias is not obvious and is not bounded.
- Minor but worth noting for anyone quoting numbers: the text reports 32,673 students / 64,162 observations while Table 1 reports 32,685 / 64,241, and the text reports 'OR = 0.0464' where Table 8 shows 0.464 and describes an OR of 0.175 as '88% lower' (it is about 82 percent lower).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the descriptive prevalence and distribution of extra credit-bearing instructional time among secondary EL-classified students in a full state population -- roughly 18 percent of student-years exceed the 0.5-credit threshold relative to same-school-grade-year non-EL peers, against a population average that is negative (-0.02 credits overall, -0.21 in core content). This is now the best available population-level evidence on the question and there is no close competitor.
- CITE IT FOR: the allocation finding -- when EL-classified students do carry more credits, that time goes disproportionately to electives and ELD rather than core content (roughly +0.61 elective credits versus +0.07 ELA and +0.03 math relative to EL peers without extra time), and 32 percent of students flagged as receiving extra time are still not enrolled in a full core course load. This is a clean, well-supported equity result that stands independent of the causal analyses.
- CITE IT FOR: the measurement idea itself. The peer-relative credit differential is a reusable instrument for detecting differential allocation of instructional time from routine administrative course records, and the paper's argument that the extra-time literature has been blind to 'fuller schedules' as a lever is a legitimate conceptual contribution worth citing on its own.
- CITE IT FOR: a well-powered null on achievement. Within-student variation in credit load produced at most 0.022 SD in ELA (core credits only) and nothing detectable in math, with standard errors tight enough (0.008 SD) to rule out policy-relevant magnitudes. Cite this as evidence that adding credits without attending to content and quality does not move test scores for this population.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: the claim that extra instructional time raises graduation. The paper's own supplementary analysis shows no effect on graduating when regular and modified diplomas are pooled; the result is diploma-type substitution, with regular-diploma odds ratios that are significant in only two of four headline specifications (one of them at p < .1) on a matched sample of roughly 1,300 students. Describe it as suggestive evidence on diploma type, as the authors do in the body, not as an attainment effect.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: an estimate of the effect of a supplemental instructional program (summer school, extended day, tutoring, credit recovery). The treatment is a credit differential relative to peers, and the authors state directly that much of it likely reflects fuller schedules rather than supplemental offerings. Citing this paper alongside program evaluations such as Kraft and Novicoff (2024) or Callen et al. (2025) as though it estimates the same parameter is a category error.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: the claim that extra time increases full-course-load enrollment or core-content credits as a causal finding. Those regressions decompose a total credit differential into its subject-area components and are close to arithmetic identities; read Table 6 as an allocation table.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: 'extra time is distributed progressively to the neediest EL students.' The subgroup pattern is mixed -- dually identified students have lower odds of extra CORE time (OR 0.751) and a negative core differential, higher English proficiency predicts more core extra time, and the dominant gradient is grade level (53 percent flagged in grade 12 versus 10 percent in grade 9), which the authors attribute partly to non-EL peers reducing their own course loads.
- GENERALIZABILITY BOUNDARY: Oregon, 2013-14 through 2018-19, pre-COVID, a state where 67 percent of districts serve under 5 percent EL students. The diploma finding in particular depends on Oregon's modified diploma, a state-specific second-tier credential; do not port it to states without an analogous option. The prevalence figure depends on the 0.5-credit threshold and on the local non-EL comparison group and is not directly comparable to program-participation rates reported elsewhere.
- OPEN QUESTIONS A READER SHOULD KNOW REMAIN: (1) how much of the measured 'extra time' is supplemental instruction versus repeated coursework after failure -- the data cannot distinguish enrolled from earned credits; (2) whether the diploma-type result survives a design with exogenous variation rather than matching on observables; (3) whether the achievement null reflects weak instruction, misallocation to electives, or the documented validity limits of English-language standardized tests for EL-classified students, three explanations the paper offers but cannot adjudicate; (4) what happens after graduation, given that the whole significance of the modified/regular distinction rests on postsecondary access; and (5) whether the peer-relative measure replicates in higher-EL-density states where non-EL scheduling norms differ.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW. Three things, in descending order of durability. First, a measurement move: extra instructional time is operationalized as a student's enrolled credits minus the mean enrolled credits of non-EL students in the same school, grade, and year, with a 0.5-credit binary threshold. This detaches the study of extra time from the existence of a named program and makes it estimable from any state's course records. Second, a population-level descriptive portrait of extra time for secondary EL-classified students that simply did not exist: prevalence, subgroup distribution, format, and subject allocation across 32,673 students and about 64,000 student-years. Third, a set of effect estimates of varying credibility. The first two are the contribution. The third is where the paper's rhetoric outruns its evidence.

THE CONSTRUCT PROBLEM, AND WHY IT PROPAGATES. The authors are admirably explicit in the discussion: 'we suspect that many students that we identified as receiving "extra" instruction simply had fuller high school schedules,' and state leaders told them EL students may have LESS access to genuinely supplemental programming than peers. This is not a footnote-sized caveat; it changes what every downstream number means. The grade gradient makes the point concrete. Extra-time (any) prevalence runs 15, 14, 16 percent in grades 6-8, drops to 10 percent in grade 9, then jumps to 37 percent in grade 11 and 53 percent in grade 12 -- and the paper explains the jump itself: non-EL students who have banked their 24 credits reduce their loads late in high school, lowering the comparison mean. So a substantial share of the flagged 'treatment' in the grades that drive the graduation analysis is the comparison group leaving, not the EL student receiving anything additional. Note also that grade 12 mean total credits for EL students with extra time (6.11 overall in grade 12 per Table 2) is LOWER than in grade 9 (7.02); the differential is positive because peers fell faster. The abstract's framing -- 'schools can offer EL-classified students additional instructional time through longer school days, fuller schedules, or summer school... roughly one in five EL-classified students received extra time' -- invites readers to hear 'one in five got a program.' They did not. Relatedly, the 86 percent 'longer school day' format figure is definitional: longer day is the residual assigned when summer, online, and concurrent enrollment are not observed, and summer and online are acknowledged to be undercounted. The finding is better stated as 'extra credits are almost entirely accumulated inside the regular school year at the student's own school,' which is still interesting and still supports the fuller-schedules reading.

RANKING THE ANALYSES BY WHAT THEY CAN BEAR. (1) The subject-allocation comparison (Table 5) is a simple mean difference and is the most trustworthy substantive result: extra time goes mostly to electives (+0.61 credits total, +0.95 in grade 12) with small core gains, and 32 percent of recipients still lack a full core load. This is the finding I would most want the field to carry forward, and it cuts against the paper's own optimistic conclusion. (2) The achievement models are the best-identified estimates in the paper -- student, grade-by-year, and school fixed effects, exploiting within-student variation in credit load -- and they are precise nulls. Note the pattern across models is itself informative: the ELA 'any' coefficient falls from 0.028 (student FE only) to 0.012 once grade-by-year and school FE and time-varying covariates enter, which is exactly what one expects if the raw association is largely composition. (3) The course-taking models share that design but ask a question whose answer is nearly determined by construction; the subject components sum to about 0.88 of each additional credit. (4) The graduation models are the weakest link and, unfortunately, the source of the headline. They abandon fixed effects for coarsened exact matching on observables, dichotomize a continuous treatment because continuous-treatment weighting methods 'did not find strong covariate balance' (an admission that the propensity model was not well behaved), and run on matched samples of roughly 845 to 1,383. Across the four headline regular-diploma cells, two are non-significant, one is p < .1, and one is p < .05, with no consistent story about whether 'any' or 'core' time is what matters. The authors call these results 'exploratory' and 'tentative causal estimates.' The abstract calls them 'substantially increased.'

THE DIPLOMA SUBSTITUTION POINT DESERVES EMPHASIS. Supplementary Table A7 -- reported in one sentence in the results -- shows that when regular and modified diplomas are combined, nothing is significant: the positive regular-diploma effects and negative modified-diploma effects cancel. So the credible version of the claim is that among EL-classified students who graduate, extra core-content time is associated with earning the regular rather than the modified credential. That is a genuinely interesting and equity-relevant claim, because Oregon's modified diploma forecloses four-year college enrollment, and because EL students are two to five times over-represented among its recipients. But it is a claim about credential sorting, not about graduating. It also raises a question the paper does not ask: is this the extra time working, or is it that students with modified-diploma trajectories carry lighter, less credit-dense schedules by design (the modified diploma has fewer credit requirements), which mechanically makes them non-recipients of 'extra time'? That is close to reverse causation running through the outcome's own definition, and matching on pre-ninth-grade covariates does not address it.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE EQUITY NARRATIVE. The discussion and conclusion assert that extra time 'is distributed progressively,' naming newcomers, long-term ELs, and ELs with disabilities. Table 3 supports this only for the 'any' specification. For core content -- the version that matters for the paper's own argument about content access and that drives the diploma result -- dually identified students have 25 percent lower odds (OR 0.751) and a significantly negative credit differential (-0.183), and students with higher math achievement have lower odds (OR 0.855) while those with higher English proficiency have higher odds (OR 1.177). Supplementary analysis reported in the text also identifies ELs with disabilities as among the groups most likely to have extra time that DISPLACES core content. A reader citing 'extra time is progressively distributed to ELs with disabilities' would be citing the abstract-level summary against the paper's own core-content table.

STANDING IN THE LITERATURE. On its central descriptive question -- which EL-classified students in a whole state carry more credits than their peers, in what format, and toward which subjects -- this is now the reference and will remain so until another state replicates it. On the causal question of whether extra instructional time helps EL students, it does not displace anything: Kraft and Novicoff's (2024) synthesis, Callen et al. (2025), and program-specific evaluations rest on stronger designs and cleaner treatments. Its most valuable causal contribution is arguably the precise null on achievement, which sharpens the field's understanding that credits are not learning time. Its most valuable conceptual contribution is the observation that schedule fullness is an unmeasured allocation lever that the extended-learning-time literature has ignored -- a claim I expect to be cited more, and more usefully, than any of the effect estimates.

HOW THE PAPER WILL LIKELY BE MISCITED. Predictably: 'Extra instructional time increases high school graduation for English learners (Umansky et al., 2026).' That sentence is not supported. The defensible versions are: 'about one in six to one in five EL-classified student-years in Oregon involved carrying more credits than same-school non-EL peers, while the EL population on average carried fewer core-content credits'; 'when EL-classified students carried extra credits, most of that time went to electives and ELD'; 'within-student increases in credit load produced no policy-relevant test-score gains'; and 'matched-comparison evidence suggests extra core-content time may shift EL students from Oregon's modified diploma toward a regular diploma, with no detectable effect on graduating overall.'

WHY 'ADEQUATE' RATHER THAN 'STRONG' OR 'WEAK.' Not weak: the question matters, the measure is genuinely novel and reusable, the descriptive evidence is population-level and new, the limitations section is honest, and at least two findings (allocation to electives, the achievement null) are both credible and consequential. Not strong: the paper's headline framing rests on the analysis it can least support, the central construct is acknowledged by the authors to be ambiguous between two very different phenomena, the effect estimates that are statistically strongest are close to mechanical, and the most striking result is bounded by an Oregon-specific credential structure that the paper does not flag as a generalizability limit. The gap between the abstract and the body is wide enough that a reader who reads only the abstract will come away with a materially wrong impression of what was demonstrated -- which is precisely the situation a reader's guide exists to correct.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper names its data source (Oregon Department of Education statewide longitudinal administrative records, 2013-14 through 2018-19) and its funder (IES R305C200008), prints all four estimating equations, and defers a substantial amount of construction detail to seven supplementary appendix tables plus an appendix on format definitions. But it carries no data availability statement, no replication package, no posted code, and no named software or estimation commands, and the main text contains several internal inconsistencies that a reader cannot resolve: the Data section's sample counts do not match Table 1 or Table 2, the analytic Ns in Tables 3 and 6-8 are never reconciled with the descriptive sample, the reported CEM retention rates cannot be squared with the Table 8 Ns, and the paper gives two flatly different definitions of the 'displacement' construct behind a headline descriptive statistic. Restricted data legitimately preclude public posting, but the combination of no access pathway, no code, and unreconcilable sample sizes means the central estimates are effectively unverifiable as reported.

**Strengths:**

- The data source is precisely and unambiguously named: statewide longitudinal student-level administrative data from the Oregon Department of Education, covering grades 6-12 for 2013-14 through 2018-19, comprising demographics, school and teacher characteristics, and course enrollment records. The provenance relationship (a state-agency partnership under the National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners) is disclosed in the Method section and again in the acknowledgements, and the funding note gives the exact IES grant number (R305C200008 to WestEd), which is the single most useful handle a would-be replicator has for locating the data management plan and related deposits.
- All four estimating equations are printed rather than described in prose, with the estimand named in each case (Equations 1 and 2 for who receives extra time; Equation 3 for the student fixed-effects models; Equation 4 for the CEM-weighted logistic graduation model). Clustering is stated for each family of models (school level for Equations 1-2, student level for Equation 3, robust for Equation 4), and the Model 1 / Model 2 / Model 3 progression in Tables 6 and 7 is defined in the table notes rather than left implicit, so the incremental logic of the specification build-up is legible.
- The core novel construct is described at an unusual level of operational detail for a journal article. The paper states the comparison set (all non-EL peers in the same grade, school, and year, with year including summer courses), the credit metric (a full-year course equals one credit, a semester course 0.5), the enrollment inclusion rule (a student counts as enrolled only if enrolled for more than 50 percent of the course's duration), the binary threshold (at least 0.5 credits above the peer mean) and the stated rationale for it, and the two subject scopes ('any' versus 'core' = ELA, math, science, social studies). A replicator would know what the authors were trying to build even if not exactly how they built it.
- The four instructional-format indicators are operationalized concretely in the Table 4 note rather than being left to the appendix alone: summer courses are courses starting June through August 31 or ending July 1 through September 30 with a duration under 150 days; online/virtual is a 'web' course location and/or a state-identified online school; concurrent enrollment is simultaneous credit-earning at more than one school; longer school day is the residual case. These are the kinds of date-window and string-match rules that are usually omitted entirely.
- Measurement limitations of the source data are disclosed candidly and specifically rather than in boilerplate: the authors state that summer and online course reporting is likely under-reported by districts, that they verified this through descriptive analyses and participant checks with state and district leaders, that the Table 4 format estimates should therefore be read as lower bounds, and that Oregon's data do not record whether students actually earned the credits they enrolled in. They also note that the assessment transitions (ELPA to ELPA21; OAKS to Smarter Balanced) required harmonization. Naming these gaps lets a reader calibrate which findings are fragile even without access to the data.
- The documentation apparatus is unusually extensive by article standards: seven supplementary appendix tables (A1 graduation requirements, A2 graduation sample descriptives before and after matching, A3 reclassification CEM models, A4 assessment harmonization procedure, A5 inverse-probability-weighting results on the continuous treatment, A6 supplement/displace tabulations, A7 combined-diploma results) plus Appendix B on format operationalization. Notably, A5 reports the alternative continuous-treatment estimator the authors rejected, and the main text explains why (poor covariate balance) rather than silently dropping it -- disclosure of a discarded specification is a real transparency asset.
- The CEM coarsening scheme is stated exactly: exact matches required on special education status, newcomer status, FRPL eligibility, cohort, gender, and race/ethnicity, and on prior math and reading proficiency levels with missing test scores treated as their own category; quintile matching on ELP scale scores. The doubly-robust second stage is also specified (all matching variables re-entered as controls, plus named instructional levers, ninth-grade school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects, robust SEs). CEM is deterministic, so no random seed is needed -- one of the few places where the absence of a stochastic-detail report is not a gap.
- The study window (2013-14 through 2018-19) deliberately ends before the pandemic, and the paper says so implicitly through the sample definition; this removes a large class of confounding that a replicator would otherwise have to reason about.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement anywhere in the article. The back matter contains ORCID iDs, a funding note, and a conflict-of-interest declaration, but no statement of where the data live, whether they can be obtained, or how. Restricted state administrative data cannot be posted publicly, and that is not itself a failing -- but the paper does not point to ODE's research data request process, does not describe the data-sharing agreement under which the authors obtained the files, does not say which files or extracts were provided, and does not say whether the agreement permits sharing derived analytic code or aggregate intermediate outputs. A reader who wants to reproduce this study has no documented pathway to start from, only a state agency's name.
- There is no replication package, no posted analysis code, and not even a 'code available upon request' offer. Nothing in the article identifies the statistical software or the estimation routines used -- no mention of Stata or R, no named commands for the linear or conditional-logit fixed-effects models, and no named CEM implementation (the cem package, MatchIt, Stata's cem, or hand-coded strata). Given that the paper's key construct is a bespoke credit-differential variable built from raw course records with date-based inclusion rules, the code is the documentation; its absence means the construction is knowable only from the narrative.
- The sample counts do not reconcile across the paper. The Data section states 32,673 students and 64,162 student-year observations; Table 1 reports 32,685 students and 64,241 student-year observations, and Table 2's total row also reports 64,241. Table 1 and Table 2 are internally consistent with each other (11,881 + 52,360 = 64,241; 5,450 + 27,235 = 32,685; the EL-subgroup, FRPL, race, grade, and ELP-level breakdowns in Table 2 each sum exactly to 64,241), so the Data-section figures appear to be from a different vintage of the file. A replicator has no way to know which N is the target.
- The analytic Ns for every regression table are unexplained and substantially smaller than the descriptive sample, with no note reconciling them. Table 3 reports N = 53,311 for all four Equation 1/2 models -- roughly 11,000 observations below Table 1's 64,241 -- with no statement of what was dropped or why, and no obvious listwise-deletion rule that produces that number (Table 1 shows 56-57 percent missingness on math and reading achievement, so deletion on the continuous z-scores would drop far more, while deletion on ELP alone would drop far less). Table 6 reports 26,461 middle-school and 12,104 high-school observations against Table 2's 38,180 (grades 6-8) and 26,061 (grades 9-12). Table 7 reports 27,476 (ELA) and 27,336 (math) against 43,919 student-years in the tested grades 6, 7, 8, and 11. Singleton-student dropping in the fixed-effects models is the plausible explanation -- the Data section says only 52 percent of students had multiple observations -- but the paper never says so, and the reader cannot distinguish singleton dropping from test-score missingness from other exclusions.
- The graduation analysis Ns cannot be reconciled with the stated sample or the stated retention rates. The Data section gives a graduation sample of N = 2,130 students; the Method states that CEM 'retains 77% of the original sample for the any extra time models and 72% of the sample for the core extra time sample,' which implies roughly 1,640 and 1,534 students. Table 8 instead reports 1,383 (any, regular diploma, four-year) and 1,338 (core, regular diploma, four-year), and shows those same Ns in the 'No matching' column, where the unmatched sample should presumably be larger. The modified-diploma columns report still smaller and different Ns (1,259 and 1,136), and the five-year panels report 882, 767, 845, and 730. None of these drops is explained -- separation-driven dropping of school fixed-effect groups and cohort-eligibility for five-year outcomes are the obvious candidates, but they are not stated. Table 8 also labels these counts 'No. of student-year observations' when the graduation sample is explicitly one observation per student.
- The paper gives two mutually incompatible definitions of the 'displacement' construct behind one of its headline descriptive statistics. The Method defines extra time that displaces core content as instances where a student receiving extra time 'was not enrolled in a full course load, meaning that they were lacking one or more of the four core content area classes that year.' The Findings section reports that 32 percent of ELs receiving extra time 'were -- even with the additional time -- not in a full course load (i.e., they never enrolled in an ELA, math, science, or social studies course that year),' which describes enrollment in none of the four core areas rather than fewer than all four. These are radically different populations and cannot both produce 32 percent. The companion 'supplemental' construct is similarly unstable: the Method defines it as enrollment in 1.5 credits (the threshold operator is at least ambiguous as printed) in a single core area, while the Findings gloss it as being enrolled in 'more than one class in a given content area,' which is not the same rule for semester-length courses. The 55 percent and 32 percent figures are not reproducible from the text as written.
- The fixed-effects specification is stated inconsistently, so the headline models cannot be re-run unambiguously from the description. Equation 3 and the Table 6 note both specify student fixed effects plus grade-by-year fixed effects plus school fixed effects. The Findings text describing the preferred model instead says 'student, grade, and school by year fixed effects' -- grade main effects with school-by-year interactions. Those are materially different absorption structures with different implications for what identifies the credit-differential coefficient (school-by-year fixed effects would absorb much of the school-year peer-mean variation the treatment is constructed from). A replicator would have to guess which was actually estimated.
- The SCED-to-subject crosswalk is never provided.
