The paper says NCES School Codes for the Exchange of Data were used to classify courses into ELA, math, science, social studies, and ELD, with everything else as electives, and footnote 3 clarifies that graduation-required world languages and financial education fall into electives -- but no code ranges, no crosswalk table, and no appendix is promised for the crosswalk (A1 covers graduation requirements, not course coding). ELD in particular is a non-obvious mapping from SCED. Because every credit count, every subject-specific outcome in Tables 5 and 6, and the 'core' versus 'any' distinction that drives the paper's central contrast all flow from this classification, its absence is the single largest barrier to rebuilding the analytic file.
- Several construction decisions that materially change the treatment variable are simply unstated. It is not said whether the non-EL comparison group includes former (reclassified) EL students, who are roughly 4.3 percent of Oregon's student population and whose inclusion or exclusion shifts every peer mean. No minimum cell size is imposed or reported for the school-by-grade-by-year peer mean, so grade-school-year cells with a handful of non-EL students produce noisy benchmarks with no stated safeguard. For students concurrently enrolled in two schools (2 percent of the sample), it is not stated which school supplies the peer mean. The academic-year boundary for assigning summer courses is defined only inside the Table 4 format note, not for the credit-year construction, even though the text says 'year included summer courses.' And the mapping from course start/end dates to credit fractions is illustrated only for full-year and semester courses, leaving trimester, block, and double-period courses undefined.
- The assessment harmonization -- arguably the most consequential single processing step for the achievement results -- is entirely deferred to Supplementary Appendix Table A4, and the main text does not even summarize the approach. Nothing in the article states whether the math and reading z-scores were standardized against the full statewide grade-year distribution or only within the EL sample, which changes the meaning of the reported 0.022 SD ELA effect by a large factor. The ELPA-to-ELPA21 and OAKS-to-Smarter Balanced transitions occur mid-panel, so a replicator cannot even sanity-check whether harmonization was rank-based, scale-linked, or category-mapped.
- The described covariates do not match the reported models. The Method says the 'who gets extra time' analyses used ELP level (1-3 plus Missing) and prior-year math and reading levels (1-4 plus Missing) as categorical variables; Table 3 instead reports continuous z-scores for English proficiency, math achievement, and reading achievement, with no Missing categories. Table 3 also omits cohort, which the Method lists among the variables of interest, and omits gender entirely -- gender is used as an exact matching variable in the CEM design but appears nowhere in Table 1's descriptive statistics and nowhere in any model table, so the reader never learns the sample's gender composition or how it was coded.
- The 'longer school day' format is defined residually as any extra-credit case not flagged as summer, online, or concurrent enrollment. The finding that 86 percent of extra-time students received it through 'a longer school day' is therefore largely definitional rather than an observation of extended-day programs, and the paper's own Discussion concedes that many of these cases are probably just fuller schedules. Table 4 is easy to misread as evidence about program formats; the residual construction is disclosed only in the table note.
- Diagnostic and fit reporting is thin. The number of schools and districts is never reported even though standard errors are clustered at the school level in Equations 1-2, so the reader cannot judge whether the cluster count supports the asymptotics. No R-squared, within-R-squared, or F statistic is reported for Equations 2 or 3; BIC is reported only for the two full-load logistic models. No balance statistics appear in the main text (deferred to A2), so the CEM balance claim -- 'the final sample shows strong matches' -- is asserted rather than shown where the estimates are.
- Reporting conventions vary across exhibits in ways that impede verification. Table 6 uses a single asterisk for p < .001; Table 7 uses a single asterisk for p < .1, two for p < .01, three for p < .001; Table 8 appears to use up to four asterisks. Table 5's note collapses several conventions at once. Table 3 carries no significance legend in its note at all, only an 'Odds ratios' row marker. Table 2 labels the third achievement category 'Intermediate-advanced' where Table 1 labels the same variable's category 'Intermediate-high.' A reader moving between tables has to re-derive the convention each time.
- At least two reported numbers do not match their own tables, which undermines confidence that the exhibits and text were generated from the same run. The text describes the any-credit-differential effect on ELA as '0.010 SD units' where Table 7's Model 3 cell reads 0.012 (Model 2 reads 0.011). The text reports the four-year modified-diploma estimate as 'OR = 0.0464' where Table 8 shows 0.464 (and the accompanying '54% lower' is consistent with 0.464, not 0.0464). Separately, Table 2's reading-achievement 'Missing' cell (35,986) is identical to the math 'Missing' cell, and the reading rows sum to 63,539 rather than 64,241 while the math rows sum exactly -- Table 1's reported missingness rates (0.56 math, 0.57 reading) imply the reading figure should be roughly 36,688, so that cell appears to have been duplicated from the math row.
- The graduation treatment definition -- 'receiving 0.5 more credits than non-EL peers in 2 or more years of high school' -- is introduced with an 'e.g.,' that makes it read as an illustration rather than the operative rule, and it interacts with the panel's exit rule in a way the paper never addresses. The primary sample drops students once they are reclassified out of EL status, yet 55 percent of the graduation sample was reclassified at some point during high school. Whether the count of extra-time years was taken only over years in which the student was still EL-classified, or over all four high school years regardless of classification, is not stated -- and it mechanically determines who can be counted as treated. This is the definitional ambiguity most directly load-bearing on the paper's most-cited causal claim.
- The article carries no human-subjects or IRB statement and no preregistration or analysis-plan reference, and it does not mention the IES data management plan or any deposit obligation attached to the R305C200008 award, even though the paper's own reference list points to a public center website where related outputs are hosted.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the descriptive prevalence claims -- roughly 18 percent of EL-classified student-years above the 0.5-credit threshold, a mean deficit of 0.02 total and 0.21 core credits relative to non-EL peers -- as the most robust results in the paper. They rest on tabulations that are internally consistent across Tables 1 and 2 and on a construct whose definition, however unreproducible in its fine details, is stated clearly enough that its direction and rough magnitude are not in doubt. Do not, however, rely on any specific decimal, since the peer-group definition (whether former ELs are counted as non-EL peers) and the absence of a minimum cell size for the school-grade-year peer mean can move these values.
- Before citing the graduation results -- the paper's headline causal claim and the one the abstract leads with -- ask the authors to reconcile Table 8's Ns with the stated graduation sample of 2,130 and the stated CEM retention rates of 77 and 72 percent. Ask specifically why the 'No matching' column reports the same N as the matching columns, why the modified-diploma models have smaller Ns than the regular-diploma models, and how many school fixed-effect groups were dropped for perfect prediction. Until that reconciliation exists, the graduation estimates are effectively unverifiable, and the authors' own characterization of them as 'exploratory' and 'tentative' should be taken at face value.
- Request the SCED-to-subject-area crosswalk before attempting any replication. Nothing else in the analytic file can be rebuilt without it: every credit count, the core-versus-any contrast that carries the paper's central distinction, the subject-specific outcomes in Tables 5 and 6, and the elective category that absorbs graduation-required world languages and financial education all depend on it. Ask in particular how ELD courses were identified in SCED and whether ESL-coded, sheltered-content, and bilingual-instruction courses were treated consistently across districts and years.
- Ask the authors which fixed-effects structure was actually estimated for Tables 6 and 7: Equation 3 and the table notes specify grade-by-year plus school fixed effects, while the Findings text describes school-by-year fixed effects. This is not cosmetic -- school-by-year absorption would soak up much of the variation from which the school-grade-year peer mean is constructed, and the two specifications answer different questions. Do not attempt to re-run the models until this is settled.
- Do not cite the 55 percent 'supplemental' and 32 percent 'displacement' statistics without asking which definition produced them. The Method (lacking one or more of four core classes) and the Findings gloss (never enrolled in any of the four) cannot both be right, and the two rules would yield very different numbers. The same caution applies to the 'full academic course load' outcome in Table 6, which is never given an explicit credit threshold anywhere in the article.
- Read the achievement effect of 0.022 SD only after establishing the standardization reference from Supplementary Appendix Table A4. Whether scores were standardized against the full statewide grade-year distribution or within the EL sample changes the substantive meaning of that coefficient substantially, and the main text does not say. If A4 does not resolve it, treat the achievement null as a statement about within-EL relative position rather than about absolute learning, and note that the text's '0.010' does not match Table 7's 0.012.
- Verify the reading-achievement row of Table 2 before using its subgroup breakdowns. The 'Missing' cell (35,986) is identical to the math 'Missing' cell, the reading rows do not sum to the sample total while the math rows do, and Table 1's own missingness rates imply the reading figure should be closer to 36,700. This looks like a transcription error rather than a substantive one, but it means the reading subgroup percentages in that panel should be recomputed rather than quoted.
- Note the two discrepant sample counts (32,673 students / 64,162 observations in the Data section versus 32,685 / 64,241 in Tables 1 and 2) and ask which file the published estimates came from. The gap is small enough to be immaterial substantively but large enough to indicate that the text and the exhibits were not regenerated together, which is a reason for extra caution about the numbers in the text that lack a table cell to check them against.
- For any replication attempt, budget for the fact that the analytic samples cannot be rebuilt to exact Ns from the article. Expect to guess on at least: singleton-student handling in the fixed-effects estimation (Table 3's 53,311 and Table 6's 26,461 and 12,104 are otherwise unexplained), whether Equation 1/2 used categorical achievement levels with a Missing category as the Method says or continuous z-scores as Table 3 shows, the treatment of concurrent enrollees in the peer-mean denominator, and the academic-year boundary for summer courses. Plan to report a range of estimates across these forks rather than a single point comparison.
- Approach the ODE data through the department's own research data request process and expect a separate data-sharing agreement; do not assume the authors can share their extract. Ask the authors instead for the analytic code, the SCED crosswalk, a variable-construction codebook, and the named software and estimation commands -- none of which is restricted by student-privacy law and all of which is missing from the article. Ask also whether the IES award (R305C200008) carries a data management plan or deposit obligation that has produced a public archived version.
- Triangulate rather than replicate where possible. The same research team's related outputs on the same Oregon data -- Umansky et al. (2024) on ELD crowd-out and course access, and Bromley et al. (2025) on dually identified students' course-taking and graduation -- plus the center's public site (elrdcenter.wested.org) are the most accessible route to checking whether the credit-differential construct behaves consistently across studies and whether the sample-construction rules are documented more fully elsewhere.
- Read Table 4 as a decomposition of a residual, not as programmatic evidence. 'Longer school day' is defined as any extra-credit case not flagged as summer, online, or concurrent enrollment, so the 86 percent figure is largely mechanical. The authors themselves conclude that much of what they classify as extra time is probably fuller schedules rather than supplemental programming; the format table should not be cited as evidence that Oregon schools operated extended-day programs for EL-classified students.
- Treat the summer and online participation rates (5.0 and 1.4 percent for any extra time; 2.4 and 1.0 percent for core) strictly as lower bounds, as the authors instruct. The under-reporting is acknowledged but unquantified, and the authors' argument that it is non-differential between EL and non-EL students rests on participant checks with state and district staff rather than on any reported validation exercise, so it is not independently checkable.
- Do not rely on the Table 1 graduation rows as reported. The five-year graduation rate (0.15) is below the four-year rate (0.20) while the regular-diploma rate is identical at four and five years (0.16), and no note explains the denominators -- which cannot be the full grades 6-12 panel, since most of those students have no graduation outcome. Ask the authors for the cohort denominators before using any of these means.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Overall assessment. This is a paper whose substantive documentation is better than its infrastructural documentation, and whose narrative construction detail is better than its numerical internal consistency. The authors clearly thought carefully about how to describe a bespoke measure -- the credit differential relative to same-grade, same-school, same-year non-EL peers -- and they wrote down the pieces of it that most authors omit: the enrollment inclusion rule, the credit metric, the threshold and its rationale, the two subject scopes, and date-window definitions for the format indicators. They also disclose data-quality limitations candidly and, unusually, report that they tried a continuous-treatment estimator, failed to achieve balance, and moved to a dichotomized CEM design, with the rejected results retained in an appendix. That is genuine transparency about the analytic path.

Against that: for a 2026 article in AERA's flagship journal, there is no data availability statement, no replication package, no code, and no named software or estimation routine. Restricted state administrative data legitimately preclude posting the data, and I do not penalize that. What I do penalize is that the article gives a reader no access pathway at all -- no reference to ODE's research data request process, no description of the data-sharing agreement, no statement of what the agreement does and does not permit sharing -- and that the code, which is not restricted by any privacy law, is neither deposited nor offered. When the central construct is built by hand from raw course records using date-based inclusion rules and a course-code crosswalk, the code is not a convenience; it is the operative documentation.

Data source and access pathway. Named precisely, provenance disclosed, funder and grant number given, partnership context described. But nothing about how anyone else could obtain the files, and no human-subjects statement. The IES award (R305C200008, to WestEd) is the most useful handle a replicator has, since IES awards carry data management plan obligations, but the paper does not mention any deposit or plan.

Code, software, computational environment. Absent entirely. No language, no version, no package names, no estimation commands. This matters concretely in at least three places. First, the fixed-effects linear models: whether singleton students were dropped, and by what routine, is the most plausible explanation for the large unexplained gaps between the descriptive Ns and the Table 6 and 7 Ns, and the answer depends on the software. Second, the fixed-effects logistic models for full course load: the note says the sample is restricted to students whose full-load status changes over time, which is the signature of a conditional (Chamberlain) logit, but the estimator is never named and the interaction of a conditional logit with school and grade-by-year fixed effects is not described. Third, the CEM: which implementation, whether k-to-k matching was used, how weights were formed, and how unmatched strata were handled beyond the reported retention rates. CEM is deterministic, so at least no seed is needed -- but the IPW alternative in Appendix A5 would have stochastic and specification detail that the main text does not summarize.

Rebuilding the analytic sample. This is where a replication would stall. The paper is missing the SCED-to-subject crosswalk, without which no credit count can be reproduced -- and the crosswalk is not promised in any appendix (A1 is graduation requirements). Beyond that, the following construction forks are undocumented: whether reclassified former ELs count as 'non-EL peers' in the denominator (roughly 4.3 percent of the state's students, so a non-trivial shift in every peer mean); whether any minimum cell size was imposed on the school-by-grade-by-year peer mean; which school supplies the peer mean for the 2 percent of students concurrently enrolled at two schools; how the academic year boundary is drawn for summer courses in the credit-year assignment (the June-through-September window in the Table 4 note governs the format flag, not the credit-year assignment); and how non-standard course lengths -- trimester, block, double-period -- map to credit fractions, given that only the full-year and semester cases are illustrated. The 'more than 50 percent of course duration' enrollment rule is stated but its interaction with the credit fraction is not (does a student enrolled for 60 percent of a year-long course receive one credit or 0.6?).

Specification transparency. Equations 1 through 4 are printed, which is more than many papers do, but they are not sufficient to re-run the headline models. The most serious problem is that the fixed-effects structure is described two ways: Equation 3 and the Table 6 note say grade-by-year plus school fixed effects; the Findings text describing the preferred Model 3 says 'school by year fixed effects.' These are not equivalent, and the school-by-year variant would absorb a large share of the very school-year variation that the treatment is constructed relative to. A second problem is that the covariates described in the Method for Equations 1 and 2 (categorical ELP levels 1-3 plus Missing; categorical math and reading levels 1-4 plus Missing) are not the covariates reported in Table 3 (continuous z-scores, no Missing categories), and cohort, which is listed in the Method, does not appear in Table 3 at all. A third is that gender is used as an exact CEM matching variable but appears nowhere else -- not in Table 1's descriptives, not in any model table -- so its coding is unknown and the sample's gender composition is never reported. A fourth is that the 'full academic course load' outcome, which carries one of the paper's largest reported effects (odds ratios of 2.00 in middle school and 1.60 in high school), is never given an explicit definition with a credit threshold; the only nearby definition is the Method's displacement rule, which the Findings section then contradicts.

Internal consistency of reported Ns. The Data section reports 32,673 students and 64,162 observations. Table 1 reports 32,685 and 64,241, and Table 2's total row agrees with Table 1. Table 1 and Table 2 are internally coherent: Table 1's extra-time and no-extra-time columns sum exactly to the totals (11,881 + 52,360 = 64,241; 5,450 + 27,235 = 32,685), and Table 2's EL-subgroup, FRPL, race/ethnicity, grade, and ELP-level panels each sum exactly to 64,241. The math-achievement panel also sums exactly. The reading-achievement panel does not: it sums to 63,539, and its 'Missing' cell (35,986) is byte-identical to the math 'Missing' cell even though Table 1 reports different missingness rates for the two (0.56 versus 0.57, implying roughly 36,688 for reading). That looks like a duplicated cell. Table 3's N of 53,311 is unexplained by any obvious deletion rule. Table 6's 26,461 and 12,104 are far below the corresponding grade-band totals of 38,180 and 26,061; Table 7's 27,476 and 27,336 are far below the 43,919 student-years in the tested grades. Table 8's Ns are inconsistent with both the stated graduation sample of 2,130 and the stated 77 and 72 percent retention rates, and its 'No matching' column reports the same N as its matching columns, which should not happen if matching drops observations. Table 8 also mislabels its unit as 'student-year observations' for a sample the Data section explicitly says is one observation per student. Finally, two text-to-table mismatches appear: the text's '0.010 SD units' for the any-credit ELA effect against Table 7's Model 3 value of 0.012, and the text's 'OR = 0.0464' against Table 8's 0.464 (the accompanying '54% lower' confirms 0.464 is right and the text has a stray zero).

The reclassification exit rule and the treatment definition. This deserves separate emphasis because it bears directly on the paper's most-quoted finding. The primary panel drops students once they reclassify out of EL status -- the authors say so and explain why. The graduation sample, by contrast, includes students who reclassified during high school, and 55 percent of it did. The graduation treatment is 'receiving 0.5 more credits than non-EL peers in 2 or more years of high school.' Whether those years are counted only while the student remained EL-classified, or across all high school years regardless of classification, is never stated. Under the first reading, students who reclassified early are mechanically less likely to be counted as treated, and reclassification -- which the authors themselves show in Appendix A3 may be affected by extra time -- becomes entangled with the treatment indicator. The authors are commendably explicit that reclassification is not a pretreatment covariate and should not be matched on, and they run the reclassification models to probe it. But the underlying construction rule is left undefined, and a replicator cannot build the treatment variable without knowing it.

What is and is not checkable by a reader. Checkable: the descriptive prevalence and credit-differential means, which are consistent across Tables 1 and 2 and match the narrative; the Table 6 core-content sums, which reproduce exactly from the printed coefficients (0.108 + 0.104 + 0.054 + 0.101 = 0.367 for middle school; 0.119 + 0.115 + 0.108 + 0.088 = 0.430 for high school); the Table 2 subgroup proportions against Table 1's means. Not checkable: the analytic sample sizes for every regression table; the CEM balance claim, which is asserted in the text and shown only in an appendix; the assessment harmonization, deferred wholly to an appendix with no summary; the standardization reference for the achievement z-scores; the 55 and 32 percent supplement/displace statistics, whose two stated definitions are incompatible; and the graduation estimates, whose Ns cannot be reconciled with any stated figure.

On the appendices. Seven supplementary tables plus an appendix on format operationalization is a substantial apparatus, and I have assessed only the main text. A4 may fully document the assessment harmonization; A2 may fully document CEM balance; Appendix B may fully document format definitions; A5 and A7 report alternative estimators and combined-diploma results. If those appendices are as thorough as their descriptions suggest, several of my variable-construction concerns would soften. What they cannot fix are the problems located squarely in the main text: the absence of a data availability statement, the absence of code and software, the two discrepant sample counts, the unexplained regression Ns, the contradictory displacement definitions, the contradictory fixed-effects descriptions, the covariate mismatch between the Method and Table 3, and the text-to-table numerical mismatches. None of those is an appendix's job.

Rating rationale. I place this at 'weak' rather than 'adequate' because the missing documentation genuinely blocks verification of the central results, not merely their fine details. The graduation finding -- the paper's headline causal claim, foregrounded in the abstract -- rests on a matched sample whose size cannot be reconciled with any number the paper reports, using a treatment variable whose construction rule is ambiguous in a way that interacts with the sample's own exit rule, estimated with unnamed software under an unnamed matching implementation. The achievement finding's effect size is uninterpretable without a standardization reference the paper does not state. The course-taking findings depend on a fixed-effects structure the paper describes two incompatible ways. And the descriptive claim about displaced core content rests on a construct with two incompatible definitions. I do not reach 'insufficient' because the data source, funder, estimands, equations, and the core construct's logic are all clearly stated, the limitations are disclosed honestly, and the appendix apparatus is real -- a determined replicator with ODE data and author cooperation could get there. But they would need that cooperation, and the article alone does not supply it.

Confidence. 0.72. I can assess the main text thoroughly, and the internal-consistency findings are arithmetic and therefore firm. I cannot see Supplementary Appendix Tables A1 through A7 or Appendix B, which plausibly resolve part of the variable-construction and harmonization critique, and I cannot see whether AERJ's online version carries a data availability statement outside the article PDF's back matter. A handful of the numerical discrepancies I note could in principle be artifacts of how the article text was rendered rather than errors in the published exhibits, though the reading-achievement 'Missing' duplication and the Data-section-versus-Table-1 sample gap are hard to explain that way.
